title: Instruction Sets & Assembly
summary: What the hardware actually runs: the stored-program machine and fetch–decode–execute, RISC versus CISC encodings and addressing modes, reading x86-64 and ARM64 assembly, calling conventions and stack frames, how loops, switches, arrays and structs compile, and how code is linked, loaded and hardened with NX, ASLR and stack canaries.

lessons.title: Memory, the program counter and the instruction cycle
lessons.summary: Trace fetch, advance, decode and execute, and identify the machine’s parts.
lessons.body:
A **stored-program computer** fetches instructions encoded as numbers from memory. Changing those stored instructions changes its program. This does not require instructions and data to share a memory: both Harvard and von Neumann designs can be stored-program computers.

The **von Neumann model** uses a shared memory for code and data, making it possible for a program to produce or modify instructions using memory operations. The Manchester Baby successfully ran its first program on 21 June 1948, an early demonstration of electronic stored-program computing with read/write memory. Historical claims about a single inventor or an unqualified “first computer” are omitted here because they depend on which features count.

## The parts of the machine

This simplified von Neumann machine has a few key parts:

```
 +-----------------  CPU  ----------------+
 |  PC   (address of next instruction)    |
 |  IR   (instruction being executed)     |
 |  registers r0..rN   ALU   control unit |
 +-------------------+--------------------+
                     | address / data bus
 +-------------------+--------------------+
 | memory: one array of numbered cells    |
 |  [ code ... ][ data ... ][ stack ... ] |
 +----------------------------------------+
```

- **Memory** is one big array of numbered cells. Code and data sit side by side. The bits alone do not identify their intended use; real machines can also enforce page permissions such as execute-disable.
- The **program counter** (PC) identifies an instruction address. In our toy cycle it points at the next instruction to fetch; architectural definitions vary. x86-64 calls its instruction pointer `RIP`.
- The conceptual **instruction register** (IR) holds the fetched instruction. A real pipelined core can have many instructions in flight.
- **Registers** are a small number of very fast storage slots inside the CPU. Baseline x86-64 has 16 general-purpose integer registers (Intel APX extends this to 32); AArch64 has 31 numbered general-purpose registers, with separate rules for the stack pointer and zero register.
- The **ALU** (arithmetic logic unit) does the adding, comparing and bit-twiddling.
- The **control unit** decodes each instruction and drives everything else.

## The fetch–decode–execute cycle

Ignoring interrupts, exceptions and halted states, the toy machine repeats this cycle:

1. **Fetch.** Read the instruction at address PC from memory into IR.
2. **Advance.** Move PC on to the next instruction, which starts straight after the one just fetched:

```formula
PC_next = PC + L
where
PC_next: the new value of the program counter: the address of the next instruction to fetch
PC: the program counter: the address of the instruction that was just fetched
L: the length of that instruction: always 1 memory cell in the toy machine below, always 4 bytes on ARM64, anywhere from 1 to 15 bytes on x86-64
In words: the next instruction begins right after the end of the current one, unless the current instruction is a jump that later overwrites PC.
```

3. **Decode.** Work out what the bits mean: which operation, which registers, which memory address, any constant.
4. **Execute.** Do it: an ALU operation, a memory read or write, or a change to PC (a jump).
5. Repeat.

Jumps and branches are just instructions that write a new value into PC. A loop is a branch back to an earlier address. A function call records a return address, normally the instruction after the call, and transfers control to the callee. The exact mechanism depends on the ISA.

Because x86 instructions have variable byte lengths, starting a disassembly inside one can reinterpret its remaining bytes as another instruction or encounter an invalid encoding. Byte addresses alone do not mark intended instruction boundaries.

Real CPUs also accept **interrupts**, such as a hardware timer event. When an interrupt is eligible under the architecture’s masking and priority rules, the CPU preserves enough state to resume and transfers control to a handler. A preemptive OS can use timer interrupts to regain control from user code that never yields.

## Key takeaways
- Stored instructions change a machine’s behaviour without rewiring it.
- Fetch advances the toy PC before execution; a jump can replace it.
- Timer interrupts let a preemptive OS regain control from a user loop.

questions.prompt: What is the defining idea of a **stored-program** computer?

options.text: The program is wired into the hardware with plugboards and switches
options.explanation: That describes the *opposite*: ENIAC-style machines where reprogramming meant rewiring. The stored-program idea was invented to get rid of this.

options.text: Instructions are encoded in memory and fetched from there for execution
options.explanation: Correct. Program instructions live in memory. Sharing the same store with data is an additional property of a von Neumann design.

options.text: Instructions and data are kept in physically separate memories
options.explanation: That is the Harvard architecture, an alternative design. A stored-program machine may or may not split them; the key point is that the program lives in memory at all.

options.text: The program is stored on disk and executed directly from it
options.explanation: Disk storage is not the defining feature. Ordinary CPUs fetch instructions through their memory system; a loader or demand paging can bring executable bytes from a file into memory.

questions.workedExample: Stored-program means instructions are encoded in memory for the machine to fetch. A Harvard design can also be stored-program despite separating instruction and data memories. The shared code/data memory in the lesson is a von Neumann design choice.

questions.prompt: In the lesson’s simple fetch–decode–execute model, what does JMP 40 do?

options.text: It copies the instructions at address 40 into the instruction register in one go
options.explanation: The IR holds only the one instruction currently being executed. The jump does not load anything itself; the *next fetch* will read address 40.

options.text: It tells the memory to start sending instructions from address 40 instead of address 0
options.explanation: Memory is passive; it just answers reads. Nothing in memory tracks 'where the program is'. That state lives in the CPU's PC.

options.text: It writes 40 into the program counter, so the next fetch reads the instruction at address 40
options.explanation: Correct. All control flow (jumps, branches, calls, returns) comes down to writing a new value into the PC. The fetch step always reads from wherever the PC points.

options.text: It pauses the fetch–decode–execute cycle until address 40 is ready
options.explanation: A jump changes the next instruction address. Real implementations can incur fetch delays, but pausing until a location is ready is not the meaning of JMP.

questions.workedExample:
Walk one cycle through:
1. Fetch: copy the instruction at address PC into IR; the instruction is `JMP 40`.
2. Advance: move PC on by one cell, so it would point at the following instruction:

```formula
PC_next = PC + 1
where
PC_next: the program counter after the advance step
PC: the program counter: the address of the instruction just fetched
1: in the toy machine every instruction fills exactly one memory cell
In words: unless something changes it, the next fetch comes from the very next cell.
```

3. Decode: the opcode means jump, and the operand is 40.
4. Execute: write 40 into PC, overwriting the value from step 2.
5. The next cycle's fetch reads the cell at address 40.

So a jump is just 'write the PC'. A conditional branch writes the PC only if a condition holds; otherwise the advanced PC from step 2 stands.

questions.prompt: A user program contains a single instruction at address 7: `JMP 7`. It never makes a system call. On a preemptive operating system, how does the OS get the CPU back so other programs can run?

options.text: The compiler inserts hidden calls into the OS inside every loop
options.explanation: Native preemption does not depend on compiler-inserted calls. Some runtimes insert checks for their own scheduling, garbage collection or other purposes.

options.text: A hardware timer raises an interrupt; between instructions the CPU notices it, saves PC and jumps to the kernel's handler
options.explanation: Correct when the timer interrupt is enabled and eligible. Interrupt handling transfers control to the kernel, which can invoke its scheduler.

options.text: It cannot; the program will run until the user reboots
options.explanation: A correctly configured preemptive OS can regain control using interrupts without the program voluntarily yielding.

options.text: The CPU detects the infinite loop and automatically raises an exception
options.explanation: An ordinary branch to itself does not automatically fault. The hardware timer supplies the preemption event; general-purpose loop detection is not required.

questions.workedExample: The loop never voluntarily enters the kernel. An enabled hardware timer interrupt becomes eligible under the CPU’s masking and priority rules. Interrupt entry preserves a return point and transfers control to a handler; the scheduler can then arrange to run another task. This is a conceptual sequence, not a promise of zero interrupt latency.

questions.prompt: A disassembler starts inside a multi-byte x86-64 instruction, without knowing the intended instruction boundaries. What can happen?

options.text: An error: the disassembler refuses to decode misaligned code
options.explanation: x86 does not require a fixed instruction alignment. Decoding can start at any byte, though some resulting encodings are invalid.

options.text: The same instructions, just shifted by one byte
options.explanation: Starting within a variable-length instruction can reinterpret its remaining bytes; this is not a guaranteed shifted copy of the original stream.

options.text: It can decode different, plausible-looking instructions, or encounter an invalid encoding
options.explanation: Correct. The starting offset affects decoding. The new stream can later meet the original instruction boundaries again.

options.text: NOP instructions, because x86 pads every instruction to a fixed length
options.explanation: Instructions are not padded to a fixed length. NOPs can be placed for alignment or patching, but an arbitrary interior byte need not decode as NOP.

questions.workedExample: x86 instructions have variable length, up to 15 bytes. Starting inside one can reinterpret its tail as a new opcode, producing different instructions or an invalid encoding. Decoding may later resynchronize. Starting one byte after a function entry is not necessarily wrong: its first instruction could be one byte long.

lessons.title: Build a tiny instruction interpreter
lessons.summary: Decode decimal instructions and follow the accumulator interpreter.
lessons.body:
## A small computer in Python

The clearest way to understand the cycle is to build one. This toy machine has one register, an **accumulator** (`acc`), and memory cells holding integers. Each instruction is a single decimal number: the hundreds digit says which operation to do, and the last two digits give the memory address it works on.

```formula
ir = op × 100 + a
op = ⌊ir / 100⌋
a = ir mod 100
ir = 2 × 100 + 21 = 221
where
ir: the whole instruction as stored in one memory cell, a whole number from 0 to 699 in this machine
op: the opcode: a number from 0 to 6 that says which operation to do (see the table below)
a: the address operand: which memory cell, 0 to 99, the instruction reads, writes or jumps to
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number, so ⌊221 / 100⌋ = 2
mod: modulo: the remainder after whole-number division, so 221 mod 100 = 21
100: the machine works in decimal and gives the address two digits (00 to 99), so multiplying the opcode by 100 shifts it past them
In words: the hundreds digit is the operation and the last two digits are the address, so 221 means "ADD the value in cell 21 to the accumulator".
```

Decoding is the reverse: Python's `divmod(ir, 100)` returns the floor and the remainder together. In the table, `m[a]` means the memory cell at address `a`, written in the same Python style as the code below:

| op | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | HALT |
| 1 | `acc = m[a]` (LOAD) |
| 2 | `acc += m[a]` (ADD) |
| 3 | `acc -= m[a]` (SUB) |
| 4 | `m[a] = acc` (STORE) |
| 5 | `if acc == 0`: jump to `a` (JZ, jump if zero) |
| 6 | jump to `a` (JMP, jump) |

```python
def run(mem):
    pc, acc = 0, 0
    while True:
        ir = mem[pc]             # fetch
        # Default to the following cell.
        pc += 1
        op, a = divmod(ir, 100)  # decode
        if op == 0:              # execute
            return
        elif op == 1:
            acc = mem[a]
        elif op == 2:
            acc += mem[a]
        elif op == 3:
            acc -= mem[a]
        elif op == 4:
            # STORE can also overwrite code.
            mem[a] = acc
        elif op == 5:
            if acc == 0:
                # Branch replaces next PC.
                pc = a
        elif op == 6:
            pc = a
        else:
            raise ValueError("bad opcode")
```

This teaching interpreter assumes integer cells and valid in-range addresses. Unknown opcodes raise an error; invalid accesses can raise Python exceptions. There is no step limit, so a looping program can run forever.

## Key takeaways
- The opcode selects an operation and the address selects a memory cell.
- The accumulator collects arithmetic results.
- This teaching interpreter needs valid addresses and has no execution limit.

questions.prompt: In the toy interpreter, the accumulator holds 7, cell 21 holds 4, and the next fetched instruction is `221`. What changes during its execution?

options.text: The accumulator becomes 11.
options.explanation: Opcode 2 adds cell 21 to the accumulator.

options.text: Cell 21 becomes 7.
options.explanation: That would be STORE, opcode 4.

options.text: The accumulator becomes 221.
options.explanation: The instruction is decoded rather than used as an immediate operand.

options.text: The program jumps to cell 21.
options.explanation: A jump needs opcode 5 or 6.

questions.workedExample: Decode 221 into opcode 2 and address 21. Read the value 4 from cell 21. ADD combines it with the accumulator’s 7, leaving 11. The memory cell is unchanged. The fetch already advanced the program counter, and ADD does not replace it.

lessons.title: Trace a complete stored program
lessons.summary: Trace the summing program and see how writing code cells changes execution.
lessons.body:
This example uses the preceding toy interpreter: LOAD, ADD, SUB, STORE, JZ and JMP operate on the accumulator and numbered memory cells. Fetch advances the program counter before execution. The same `run(mem)` function executes the program below.

Here is a program that adds up every whole number from a starting value down to 1:

```formula
total = n + (n − 1) + … + 1   for n ≥ 1
total = 0   for n = 0
total = (n(n + 1)) / 2
total = 3 × 4 / 2 = 6
where
total: the sum the program leaves in memory cell 21
n: the starting value, a whole number 0 or more, stored in cell 20 (3 in the run below)
…: and so on: every whole number in between is included
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: zero has an empty sum of 0; for a positive input add n, then one less, all the way down to 1; the shortcut n × (n + 1) / 2 gives the same answer, so starting from 3 the program should end with 6.
```

The code is at addresses 0 to 8, `n` lives at 20, the running total at 21 and the constant 1 at 22:

```
addr  value  meaning
 0     120   LOAD  20     acc = n
 1     508   JZ    8      if n == 0: halt
 2     221   ADD   21     acc = n + total
 3     421   STORE 21     total = acc
 4     120   LOAD  20
 5     322   SUB   22     acc = n - 1
 6     420   STORE 20     n = acc
 7     600   JMP   0      loop
 8     000   HALT
```

```python
prog = [120, 508, 221, 421,
        120, 322, 420, 600,
        0]
# Fill addresses 9–19, then data 20–22.
mem = prog + [0] * 11 + [3, 0, 1]
run(mem)
print(mem[21])   # 6  (3 + 2 + 1)
```

Notice what is going on. The program is a list of integers in the same `mem` list as the data. `run` cannot tell `120` the instruction from `120` the number; it only treats a cell as an instruction because PC points at it. With `n = 3`, the loop body (8 instructions) runs three times, then LOAD, JZ and HALT run once more as the program stops:

```formula
F = 8n + 3
F = 8 × 3 + 3 = 27
where
F: the total number of instructions fetched before the machine halts
n: the starting value in cell 20 (here 3)
8: the loop body, addresses 0 to 7, which runs once for each value n, n − 1, …, 1
3: the final LOAD, JZ (now taken, because acc is 0) and HALT
In words: every pass round the loop costs 8 fetches, and stopping costs 3 more, so starting from 3 the machine makes 27 fetches.
```

> [!warning] Code is data, both ways
> If the program did `STORE 7`, it would overwrite its own `JMP` instruction with whatever number was in `acc`. That is **self-modifying code**. It is also how many attacks work: trick a program into writing attacker-chosen bytes into memory, then trick it into jumping there.

## Key takeaways
- The same memory list holds instructions, inputs and outputs.
- The summing loop updates both the total and the remaining input.
- Each positive input costs eight fetches, followed by three stopping fetches.

questions.prompt:
In the lesson's toy machine, the summing program is run with input 4 in memory cell 20. How many instructions are **fetched** before the machine halts?

```
 0 LOAD 20    5 SUB  22
 1 JZ   8     6 STORE 20
 2 ADD  21    7 JMP  0
 3 STORE 21   8 HALT
 4 LOAD 20
```

options.explanation: That is the count for n = 3 (the lesson's example). Each extra iteration adds 8 fetches.
This counts only the loop iterations (4 × 8) and forgets the final LOAD, JZ and HALT that run when n reaches 0.
This counts 4 iterations of 9 instructions, but the HALT at address 8 is not part of the loop body; addresses 0 to 7 are.
Correct. Four passes of the 8-instruction loop (addresses 0 to 7) is 32 fetches, then LOAD, JZ (taken) and HALT add 3.

questions.workedExample:
1. One pass through the loop executes addresses 0 to 7: 8 instructions.
2. JZ at address 1 is not taken while n is above zero, so the loop runs with n at 4, 3, 2 and 1: four passes, 4 × 8 = 32.
3. Then n has reached 0: LOAD (addr 0), JZ (addr 1, now taken), HALT (addr 8): 3 more.
4. The 32 loop fetches and three stopping fetches total **35**. The general count is:

```formula
F = 8 × n + 3
F = 8 × 4 + 3 = 35
F = 8 × 3 + 3 = 27
where
F: the number of instructions fetched before the machine halts
n: the starting value stored in cell 20
8: one pass of the loop body, addresses 0 to 7
3: the final LOAD, JZ (taken) and HALT once n is 0
In words: 8 fetches per pass round the loop plus 3 to stop, so starting from 4 gives 35 and the lesson's start of 3 gives 27.
```

questions.prompt: A bug corrupts cell 7 of the toy program, changing `600` (JMP 0) to `000`. The program then runs with `n = 3`, `total = 0`. What is `mem[21]` when it halts?

options.explanation: That is the correct sum, but it needs three trips around the loop. With cell 7 now a HALT, the loop never repeats.
Correct. The first pass adds n (3) into total and stores it, decrements n to 2, then hits the HALT at cell 7. The machine cannot tell the corrupted cell was 'meant' to be a jump.
The ADD and STORE at cells 2 and 3 run before cell 7 is reached, so total is updated once.

options.text: The machine crashes because 000 is not a valid instruction at that address
options.explanation: 000 *is* valid: opcode 0 is HALT. The CPU decodes whatever number PC points at; it has no notion of which cells were intended as code.

questions.workedExample:
Trace from PC = 0 with acc = 0:

```
0 LOAD 20   acc = 3
1 JZ 8      acc != 0, not taken
2 ADD 21    acc = 3 + 0 = 3
3 STORE 21  total = 3
4 LOAD 20   acc = 3
5 SUB 22    acc = 2
6 STORE 20  n = 2
7 (000)     HALT
```

`mem[21] = 3`. The lesson's point: code is just numbers in memory, so overwriting a code cell silently changes the program. That is self-modifying code, and also how memory-corruption bugs turn into wrong behaviour or exploits.

lessons.title: The ISA contract and shared memory paths
lessons.summary: Distinguish architectural compatibility from implementation and compare memory organisations.
lessons.body:
## What an ISA promises

The **instruction set architecture** (ISA) is the contract between software and hardware. It specifies:

- the instructions and how each is encoded in bits,
- the registers and their sizes,
- how memory is addressed (byte addressing, alignment rules, endianness),
- what happens on errors, interrupts and system calls,
- the privilege levels (user mode vs kernel mode).

The ISA deliberately does *not* say how the chip is built. That is the **microarchitecture**. AMD Zen and Intel Core designs both implement x86-64 but are very different inside. Apple's M-series and AWS Graviton chips both implement ARM64. Binary compatibility also requires the instructions and extensions actually used, a compatible OS and ABI, executable format, and required libraries. An ARM64 macOS binary does not therefore run unchanged on an ARM64 Linux server.

This separation is why your old programs still run on new hardware. A CPU must preserve the ISA’s observable behaviour. Many implementations overlap instructions (pipelining), issue several per cycle (superscalar), and execute out of order. This does not promise sequential consistency between threads: the ISA’s memory-ordering rules still apply. The next module covers how.

## Von Neumann, Harvard and the bottleneck

Because code and data share one memory and one path to the CPU, fetching instructions and loading data compete for the same memory bus. John Backus called this the **von Neumann bottleneck** in 1977. Main-memory latency and bandwidth can limit execution; caches and prefetching can reduce that pressure. A universal claim about the fraction of chip area occupied by caches is omitted because it requires measurements of a specified chip.

The alternative is the **Harvard architecture**: separate memories (and buses) for instructions and data. Many microcontrollers and DSPs work this way; on an AVR (the chip in classic Arduinos) the program sits in flash memory and data in SRAM.

A common modern general-purpose arrangement is called **modified Harvard** (the exact cache hierarchy is chip-specific):

| Level | Code and data |
|---|---|
| L1 cache | split: L1i and L1d |
| L2, L3 | unified |
| Main memory | one address space |

The split L1 lets the CPU fetch instructions and load data in the same cycle. Programmers still see one address space, while instructions and data can use separate cache paths.

## Key takeaways
- The ISA defines software-visible behaviour; microarchitecture implements it.
- Binary compatibility also needs the right extensions, ABI and operating system.
- Split instruction/data caches reduce contention without requiring separate programmer address spaces.

questions.prompt: The same Linux x86-64 binary runs unmodified on an Intel Core laptop and an AMD Ryzen desktop, whose internal designs are completely different. Why does this work? Assume both machines support the binary’s required extensions and have compatible Linux ABIs and libraries.

options.text: Both chips implement the same instruction set architecture; only their microarchitectures differ
options.explanation: Correct under the stated compatibility assumptions: the processors implement the instruction semantics the program requires, with different internal implementations.

options.text: Linux translates the binary to each chip's native instructions when it loads it
options.explanation: Ordinary native loading does not translate these instructions. Dynamic translation can be used in other contexts, including emulating a CPU with the same ISA.

options.text: AMD licenses Intel's chip design, so the two are internally the same
options.explanation: Sharing an ISA does not mean sharing an internal core design; Zen and Core are different microarchitectures.

options.text: x86-64 binaries contain several versions of the code, one per CPU vendor
options.explanation: Normal binaries contain a single version of the code. (Some libraries pick optimised routines at run time based on CPU features, but that is not why the binary runs at all.)

questions.workedExample: The binary needs compatible instruction semantics plus its OS ABI, loader and libraries. Given those assumptions, different pipeline and cache designs can execute it. ISA compatibility does not promise identical timings, CPU identification values or every nondeterministic result.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are true of a typical modern laptop or server CPU? Select all that apply.

options.text: It has separate level-1 caches for instructions (L1i) and data (L1d)
options.explanation: Correct. Splitting L1 lets the core fetch instructions and load data in the same cycle, easing the von Neumann bottleneck.

options.text: Programs see a single address space in which code and data both live
options.explanation: Code and data can inhabit the same process virtual address space, although mappings have different permissions. Split caches do not require separate programmer-visible spaces.

options.text: Code and data are kept in physically separate DRAM chips, as in a pure Harvard machine
options.explanation: That describes pure Harvard designs such as some microcontrollers. General-purpose CPUs store code and data in the same DRAM.

options.text: Instructions are executed strictly one at a time, each finishing before the next is fetched
options.explanation: Modern cores overlap instructions while preserving architectural behaviour. Their memory model still determines what concurrent threads can observe.

questions.workedExample: For the typical arrangement described: separate L1 instruction/data caches and one process address space are true. Separate code/data DRAM and strictly one-at-a-time execution are false. Cache sizes and lower cache arrangements vary by chip.

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical model a 3 GHz core needs one 4-byte instruction and 8 data bytes from DRAM per cycle, with no caches or reuse. Assume one 64-bit DDR4-3200 data channel has a theoretical peak of 25.6 GB/s and assume 80 ns access latency. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Bandwidth is fine (12 bytes per cycle is only 12 GB/s), so caches are unnecessary
options.explanation: 12 bytes per cycle at 3 × 10⁹ cycles per second is 36 GB/s, not 12 GB/s; the arithmetic dropped the clock rate. And it ignores latency entirely.

options.text: Demand is 36 GB/s, exceeding the channel peak; 80 ns is 240 cycles, which matters for dependent accesses
options.explanation: Correct: 12 bytes × 3 billion cycles/s = 36 GB/s; 80 ns × 3 cycles/ns = 240 cycles. Peak bandwidth also excludes real protocol and access-pattern losses.

options.text: It needs 36 GB/s, so adding a second memory channel (51.2 GB/s) solves the problem completely
options.explanation: A second channel can increase peak bandwidth, but does not by itself eliminate access latency, dependencies or protocol overhead.

options.text: Latency doesn't matter, because the CPU can fetch the next instruction while waiting
options.explanation: Independent requests can overlap, but dependency chains can expose latency. The bandwidth shortfall already prevents the stated sustained demand on one channel.

questions.workedExample:
Work out what the core demands, what one channel can supply, and what the latency costs in cycles:

```formula
D = d × f
D = 12 B × 3 × 10^9 /s
D = 36 × 10^9 B/s = 36 GB/s
P = w × r
P = 8 B × 3.2 × 10^9 /s = 25.6 GB/s
N = t × f
N = 80 ns × 3 cycles/ns = 240 cycles
where
D: the bandwidth the core demands from memory
d: bytes needed per cycle: a 4-byte instruction plus 8 data bytes = 12 bytes
f: the clock rate: 3 GHz, meaning 3 × 10^9 cycles every second, which is the same as 3 cycles every nanosecond
P: the channel's theoretical peak bandwidth
w: the channel width: 64 bits = 8 bytes moved per transfer
r: transfers per second: 3.2 × 10^9 for DDR4-3200
N: the access latency counted in clock cycles
t: the assumed access latency, 80 nanoseconds
B: byte, 8 bits
GB: gigabyte, 10^9 bytes
s: second
ns: nanosecond, 10^-9 of a second
cycles: clock cycles, one tick of the 3 GHz clock each
In words: the core wants 36 GB/s but the channel peaks at 25.6 GB/s, and each memory access takes as long as 240 clock ticks.
```

Overlap can hide some latency, but dependencies and finite bandwidth still constrain throughput; it is not true that every instruction necessarily waits a full DRAM latency.

lessons.title: JIT code, permissions and instruction visibility
lessons.summary: Explain why generated machine code needs permission, cache and thread coordination.
lessons.body:
## Where this matters in practice

### JIT compilers

A JavaScript engine like V8 or the JVM's HotSpot writes machine code into memory at run time and then jumps to it. That is the stored-program idea at full power. Two practical wrinkles:

- **Write xor execute (W^X).** A common policy prohibits a virtual mapping from being writable and executable simultaneously. JITs can switch permissions; simultaneous RW and RX aliases satisfy that mapping-level rule but do not prevent writable access to executable backing memory. Stronger policies may forbid those aliases. Apple’s JIT APIs use `MAP_JIT`, thread-specific write protection and, depending on the configuration, entitlements and callback allowlists; follow the current platform documentation.
- **Instruction visibility.** Generated code needs the platform’s cache-maintenance and instruction-synchronization protocol. On AArch64, use a supported cache-clear API; required maintenance depends on CPU features. Publishing or replacing code across threads also requires coordination with executing threads. x86 hardware coherence does not make arbitrary concurrent code modification safe. On Apple platforms, follow Apple’s instruction-cache invalidation guidance.

### Emulators and interpreters

The Python `run` loop resembles a simple instruction interpreter: fetch an opcode, dispatch, repeat. Faster implementations can differ substantially. For example, QEMU’s TCG backend translates blocks of guest instructions into host code instead of interpreting every guest instruction through this Python-style loop.

## Pitfalls and misconceptions

- **"The CPU knows what's code."** Bytes do not identify their intended high-level use, although execute permissions can restrict which pages may supply instructions. Starting inside an x86 instruction can produce a different decoding or an invalid opcode.
- **"One instruction per clock tick."** Not on a modern CPU. Instruction latency and throughput vary by instruction, dependencies, memory behaviour and microarchitecture. Multiple instructions can be in progress simultaneously.
- **"The ISA is the chip."** The ISA is an interface. Chips implementing the same ISA can have different performance and power characteristics; measure the relevant workload.

## Key takeaways
- Generating bytes and executing them requires both permissions and instruction visibility.
- Mapping-level W^X can permit writable and executable aliases of the same backing memory.
- Cross-thread code publication needs the platform’s coordination protocol.

## Further reading

questions.prompt: A JIT writes valid native ARM64 instructions to a buffer with appropriate executable permissions. On one ARM64 server it sometimes executes instructions previously held in that buffer. Which missing step best explains this?

options.text: ARM64 uses a different byte order, so the code bytes are reversed
options.explanation: Byte order must match the target, but the prompt supplies valid native instructions. Stale instructions point instead to instruction visibility.

options.text: The ARM64 kernel is randomising the buffer's address (ASLR)
options.explanation: ASLR picks addresses when memory is mapped; it does not change the contents of a buffer you have already written.

options.text: The JIT omitted the required instruction-cache maintenance and synchronization before executing updated code
options.explanation: Correct. Use the platform’s cache-clear API and code-publication protocol. Which explicit maintenance operations are needed depends on the CPU; sharing code across threads requires additional coordination.

options.text: ARM64 cannot execute code from memory that was ever written to
options.explanation: ARM64 can; every JIT on ARM (V8, HotSpot, LuaJIT) does it. It requires the right page permissions and cache maintenance, not avoiding writes altogether.

questions.workedExample: Stores and instruction fetches can see different cached contents. A platform cache-clear API arranges the required visibility and instruction synchronization. For multiple threads, coordinate publication and execution as well. Neither a blanket “all ARM caches are incoherent” nor “x86 code updates always work” is a reliable rule.

questions.prompt: For this question, the policy is specifically: no single virtual mapping may be writable and executable at once. Which designs meet that mapping-level W^X rule? Select all that apply.

options.text: A JIT maps one buffer read-write, fills it, then changes its permissions to read-execute before jumping into it
options.explanation: Correct. At no moment is the page both writable and executable; this flip-the-permissions approach is a standard W^X pattern.

options.text: The program's stack is mapped read-write-execute so that a legacy library can run code placed there
options.explanation: RWX violates the specified policy. It allows execution of bytes written there, although exploiting a bug also requires a way to redirect control flow.

options.text: A JIT maps the same physical memory twice: one view read-write, another view read-execute, at different addresses
options.explanation: Each mapping meets this narrow rule, but the writable alias can still change executable backing memory. A stronger policy may prohibit such simultaneous aliases.

options.text: A JIT keeps one buffer permanently read-write-execute for speed
options.explanation: RWX violates the specified policy. Combining writable executable memory with a suitable write and control-flow primitive can allow code injection.

questions.workedExample: RW then RX complies with the stated mapping-level rule; RWX mappings do not. Separate RW and RX aliases also meet this narrow rule, but are weaker than a policy forbidding simultaneous writable access to executable backing memory. Hiding an alias is not a security guarantee.

lessons.title: RISC, CISC and load/store organisation
lessons.summary: Compare the same non-atomic update on x86-64 and AArch64.
lessons.body:
An instruction is a number. The earlier toy machine put the operation in the hundreds digit of a decimal number and the address in the last two digits. Real ISAs pack the operation, registers, constants and addressing information into bit fields. How they do that, and how much one instruction is allowed to do, splits ISAs into two broad families.

## Two philosophies

**CISC** (complex instruction set computer) is the older style: VAX, Motorola 68000, and Intel x86. In the 1970s memory was expensive and compilers were weak, so designers made each instruction do a lot. One instruction could load from memory, do arithmetic and store the result. Instructions had many lengths, so common ones could be short.

**RISC** (reduced instruction set computer) grew from research in the 1970s and 1980s, including IBM's 801, Berkeley RISC (which led to SPARC) and Stanford MIPS. Their measurements showed compilers mostly used simple instructions anyway. So they designed ISAs that were:

- **Load/store**: ordinary ALU operations use registers/immediates, with separate memory-transfer instructions. Atomic read-modify-write instructions are an important extension.
- **Fixed-length encoding**: often a 32-bit base encoding, simplifying boundary detection; compressed extensions are exceptions.
- **Register-rich**: typically a relatively large register file, reducing register spills; exact counts vary by ISA.
- **Regular**: few formats, so the hardware is simple and easy to pipeline.

ARM64 (AArch64), RISC-V, MIPS and POWER are RISC. x86-64 is CISC.

### The same statement both ways

Take `a[i] += 1` where `a` points to 32-bit integers, the index is in range and the increment does not overflow a signed C `int`. These are ordinary non-atomic updates. On x86-64 one instruction does it, with a memory operand:

```
# rdi = a, rsi = i
add  dword ptr [rdi + rsi*4], 1
```

Using ordinary AArch64 load, add and store instructions takes three:

```
// x0 = a, x1 = i
ldr  w8, [x0, x1, lsl #2]   // w8 = a[i]
add  w8, w8, #1
str  w8, [x0, x1, lsl #2]   // a[i] = w8
```

The shown x86 encoding is 4 bytes; the A64 sequence is 12. The x86 instruction still requires a read, arithmetic and a write internally; the number and fusion of micro-ops depend on the core. A single memory-operand instruction is not automatically an atomic inter-thread increment.

> [!note] "Reduced" is about complexity, not count
> RISC does not mean few instructions. ARM64 has hundreds, including SIMD, crypto and atomics. The label describes design tendencies, not a rule that every instruction does only one simple operation. AArch64 includes atomic read-modify-write and other specialized operations.

## Key takeaways
- RISC and CISC describe design traditions rather than performance rankings.
- Ordinary AArch64 arithmetic uses registers and separate loads/stores.
- A single x86 memory update still performs a read, arithmetic and a write.

## Further reading

questions.prompt: Which of these is a defining property of a **load/store** (RISC) architecture such as ARM64?

options.text: It has fewer than 100 instructions in total
options.explanation: RISC is about simplicity and regularity, not a small count. ARM64 has hundreds of instructions once SIMD, crypto and atomics are included.

options.text: It cannot address more than 4 GB of memory
options.explanation: AArch64 uses 64-bit general-purpose address operands, with implemented virtual and physical address widths depending on architectural features and configuration. ADRP reach is not a whole-memory limit.

options.text: Every instruction completes in exactly one clock cycle
options.explanation: Early RISC designs aimed for one instruction per cycle *throughput* in a pipeline, but loads that miss the cache, divisions and many other instructions take much longer.

options.text: Ordinary ALU instructions use registers/immediates rather than memory operands; memory transfers use separate instructions
options.explanation: Correct for ordinary arithmetic such as ADD. Atomic read-modify-write instructions are an important specialized exception to an overbroad “only plain loads/stores access memory” rule.

questions.workedExample: Load/store organization separates ordinary ALU arithmetic from memory transfers. It does not impose a small instruction count, a 4 GB address-space limit or one-cycle completion, and modern extensions include atomic memory operations.

lessons.title: Read an A64 instruction’s bit fields
lessons.summary: Decode the fields of a concrete A64 add/sub instruction.
lessons.body:
## Fixed-length encoding: ARM64

Every A64 instruction is exactly 32 bits. Here is `add x0, x0, x1`, which assembles to `0x8b010000`:

```
0x8b010000 = add x0, x0, x1

bits   field  value   meaning
31     sf     1       64-bit (x regs)
30     op     0       add (1 = sub)
29     S      0       don't set flags
28-24  fixed  01011   add/sub, shifted reg
23-22  shift  00      LSL
21     -      0
20-16  Rm     00001   x1
15-10  imm6   000000  shift amount 0
9-5    Rn     00000   x0
4-0    Rd     00000   x0
```

The general-purpose register fields in this format are 5 bits: encodings 0–30 name numbered registers, while 31 has instruction-dependent special meaning. The number of registers a field can name doubles with every bit:

```formula
R = 2^b
R = 2^5 = 32
where
R: the number of distinct bit patterns in the register field; one pattern has instruction-dependent special meaning
b: the width of the register field, in bits
In words: a 5-bit field has 32 possible patterns: 0 to 30 pick x0 to x30, and 31 picks the stack pointer or the zero register, depending on the instruction; the shifted-register form shown uses the zero register.
```

Regular field placement helps decoding, but not every A64 instruction uses this format. An exact Apple M1 decode-width claim is omitted because a primary hardware specification establishing it was not available in this review.

## Key takeaways
- Every A64 instruction is four bytes.
- The shown shifted-register format encodes its operation and three register fields.
- A five-bit register field has 32 patterns, with instruction-specific meaning for 31.

questions.prompt:
An ARM64 add/sub (shifted register) instruction is `0xcb020020`. In binary, with the fields separated:

```
sf op S fixed shift 0 Rm    imm6
1  1  0 01011 00    0 00010 000000
Rn    Rd
00001 00000
```

What instruction is it?

options.text: `add x0, x1, x2`
options.explanation: The `op` bit is 1, which selects subtract, not add.

options.text: `sub x0, x1, x2`
options.explanation: Correct. sf is 1 (64-bit x registers), op is 1 (subtract), S is 0 (flags untouched), Rm selects x2, Rn selects x1, Rd selects x0: subtract x2 from x1 into x0.

options.text: `sub x2, x1, x0`
options.explanation: This reads the register fields in the wrong order. Rd (bits 4–0) is the destination: 00000 = x0. Rm (bits 20–16) = x2 is the second source.

options.text: `subs w0, w1, w2`
options.explanation: S is 0 means flags are not set, so it is `sub`, not `subs`. And sf is 1 selects 64-bit x registers, not w.

questions.workedExample:
Read each field:
1. sf is 1: 64-bit, so `x` registers.
2. op is 1: subtract.
3. S is 0: do not set flags (so `sub`, not `subs`).
4. Rm is 00010, selecting x2 (second source).
5. Rn is 00001, selecting x1 (first source).
6. Rd is 00000, selecting x0 (destination).
7. imm6 is 0: no shift on Rm.

So it is `sub x0, x1, x2`. Regular placement of register fields helps decoding; actual hardware cost depends on the implementation.

lessons.title: A64 immediates and building constants
lessons.summary: Choose between immediate fields, move-wide sequences and literal pools.
lessons.body:
### The price: immediates

A 32-bit instruction cannot encode every possible 64-bit constant. ARM64 offers several immediate formats:

| Instruction | Immediate allowed |
|---|---|
| `add`/`sub` | 12 bits (0–4095), optionally shifted left 12 |
| 64-bit `movz`/`movk` | 16 bits, placed at bit 0, 16, 32 or 48 |
| Immediate `and`/`orr` | repeated, rotated runs of ones and zeros within power-of-two-sized elements; neither all-zeros nor all-ones values are encodable |
| Unsigned-offset scalar `LDR`/`STR` | 12 bits, scaled by access size; other addressing forms differ |

How big can an unsigned immediate be? A field of k bits has 2 to the power k patterns, and the smallest is 0:

```formula
v_max = 2^k − 1
v_max = 2^12 − 1 = 4096 − 1 = 4095
v = imm12 × 2^12
v = 3 × 4096 = 12288
where
v_max: the largest value an unsigned k-bit field can hold
k: the width of the immediate field, in bits: 12 for add/sub
v: the constant actually added when the "shifted left 12" option is used
imm12: the 12-bit immediate field written in the instruction, 0 to 4095
2^12: 4096: shifting a number left by 12 bits multiplies it by 2^12
In words: 12 bits reach 0 to 4095; the shifted form multiplies the field by 4096, so it reaches exact multiples of 4096 up to 4095 × 4096 = 16,773,120.
```

So `add x0, x0, #4095` is one instruction but `#4097` will not assemble: 4097 is above 4095 and is not a multiple of 4096. A full 64-bit constant takes up to four instructions:

```
mov   x0, #0xcdef            // movz
movk  x0, #0x90ab, lsl #16   // keep rest
movk  x0, #0x5678, lsl #32
movk  x0, #0x1234, lsl #48
// x0 = 0x1234567890abcdef
```

Each `movk` drops a 16-bit chunk into place without disturbing the rest, so the register ends up holding:

```formula
x0 = c_0 + c_1 × 2^16
   + c_2 × 2^32 + c_3 × 2^48
where
x0: the 64-bit register being built
c_0, c_1, c_2, c_3: the four 16-bit chunks, lowest first: 0xcdef, 0x90ab, 0x5678 and 0x1234 (0x marks a hexadecimal number)
2^16, 2^32, 2^48: the place values of bit positions 16, 32 and 48: `lsl #16` (logical shift left by 16 bits) multiplies a chunk by 2^16 = 65,536
In words: the 64-bit constant is four 16-bit pieces placed side by side, each moved to its slot by a shift.
```

MOV aliases are assembler spellings for encodable instruction forms; they are not a promise that an arbitrary constant expands automatically into a sequence. A rejected immediate requires an explicit supported sequence.

Some odd-looking constants are cheap: `0xff00ff00ff00ff00` is a repeating pattern, so it fits one `orr`-based `mov`. Compilers also put large constants in a nearby **literal pool** and load them with one PC-relative `ldr`.

## Key takeaways
- Immediate encodings cannot represent every 64-bit value.
- ADD immediates use twelve bits with an optional twelve-bit shift.
- MOVZ and MOVK can assemble any 64-bit constant from sixteen-bit chunks.

questions.prompt: Which of these would **not** be a valid ARM64 instruction?

options.text: `add x0, x1, x2`
options.explanation: Valid: it adds the two source registers and writes the result into the distinct destination register.
Valid: a load from base + displacement, the normal way to read a struct field.

options.text: `add w0, w0, [x1]` (add a value from memory)
options.explanation: Correct, this is the invalid one. Ordinary A64 ADD is a register/immediate operation and cannot take this memory operand. You would `ldr w9, [x1]` first and then `add w0, w0, w9`.

options.text: `str w8, [x0, x1, lsl #2]`
options.explanation: Valid: a store using base + scaled index, the array-element form `a[i] = w8` for 4-byte elements.

questions.workedExample: The ordinary A64 ADD instruction accepts register/immediate operands, not the bracketed memory operand in option 3. LDR followed by ADD performs the proposed load-and-add. This statement does not exclude specialized atomic read-modify-write instructions.

questions.prompt: Which of these ARM64 instructions assemble as a **single** 32-bit instruction? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. 4095 fits the 12-bit unsigned immediate of `add`.
Correct. 4096 is 1 << 12, and `add` allows its 12-bit immediate to be shifted left by 12, so it encodes as `add x0, x0, #1, lsl #12`.
4097 needs 13 bits and is not a multiple of 4096, so neither immediate form fits. You need to materialise it in a register first, or use two adds.
0x12345 spans more than 16 bits and isn't a repeating bitmask, so it needs `movz` plus a `movk` (two instructions).

options.text: `mov x0, #0xff00ff00ff00ff00`
options.explanation: Correct, surprisingly. It is a repeating 16-bit pattern, which the logical 'bitmask immediate' format can encode, so it becomes one `orr`-style instruction.

questions.workedExample:
Check each against the immediate forms. For `add`, the 12-bit field and its shifted form give:

```formula
v_max = 2^12 − 1 = 4095
v = imm12 × 2^12
v = 1 × 4096 = 4096
where
v_max: the largest unshifted immediate
v: the constant added when the field is shifted left by 12 bits
imm12: the 12-bit immediate field, 0 to 4095
2^12: 4096: shifting left by 12 bits multiplies by this
In words: add accepts 0 to 4095 directly, or a multiple of 4096 up to 4095 × 4096; 4096 itself is 1 shifted left by 12.
```

In the summary below, `<<` means shift left:

```
add imm: 0..4095, optionally << 12
movz/movk: one 16-bit chunk each
bitmask: repeating rotated runs of 1s
```

1. 4095: fits 12 bits. One instruction.
2. 4096 = 1 << 12: shifted form. One.
3. 4097 = 0x1001: not 12 bits, not a multiple of 4096. No.
4. 0x12345 = 0x1 (bits 16+) and 0x2345: two 16-bit chunks, not a pattern. Two instructions.
5. 0xff00 repeated four times: a bitmask immediate. One.

questions.prompt: You need the 64-bit constant `0x1234567890abcdef` in a register. Compare code bytes: x86-64 `movabs` is 2 bytes of opcode plus an 8-byte immediate. ARM64 can use either four `movz`/`movk` instructions, or one PC-relative `ldr` from an 8-byte literal pool entry. How many bytes does each approach use in total? Count only instruction bytes and one constant, ignoring alignment padding, branch-around code and pool sharing.

options.text: x86: 10; ARM64 movz/movk: 16; ARM64 literal pool: 12
options.explanation: Correct. movabs: 2 + 8 = 10 bytes. Four 4-byte instructions: 16 bytes. Literal load: 4-byte `ldr` + 8-byte constant = 12 bytes (and the pool entry can be shared by several uses).

options.text: x86: 8; ARM64 movz/movk: 8; ARM64 literal pool: 8
options.explanation: This counts only the constant, ignoring the opcode bytes and the fact that each ARM64 instruction is 4 bytes carrying only 16 bits of the constant.

options.text: x86: 10; ARM64 movz/movk: 4; ARM64 literal pool: 4
options.explanation: For this particular constant, the stated move-wide sequence uses four instructions. Some other 64-bit constants fit one encoded pattern, so “64-bit value” alone does not prove four are necessary.

options.text: x86: 15; ARM64 movz/movk: 16; ARM64 literal pool: 8
options.explanation: 15 bytes is x86's *maximum* instruction length, not the size of movabs. And the literal approach still needs the 4-byte `ldr` instruction.

questions.workedExample: The specified x86 encoding is 2 + 8 = 10 bytes. Four A64 instructions occupy 16 bytes. One literal LDR plus one 8-byte constant uses 12 bytes before padding or branch-around code. The load has memory-system costs; sharing a literal can amortize its data bytes. These counts do not determine which approach is faster.

lessons.title: Decode variable-length x86 instructions
lessons.summary: Read REX, opcode and ModRM bytes and compare encoding trade-offs.
lessons.body:
## Variable-length encoding: x86-64

x86 instructions are anywhere from 1 to 15 bytes. A common legacy/REX encoding uses these pieces. This is a schematic, not the complete encoding grammar: VEX, EVEX and APX/REX2 add other forms, and not every combination below is valid.

```
field      size     purpose
prefixes   varies   lock, rep, size...
REX        0-1 B    64-bit, r8-r15
opcode     1-3 B    the operation
ModRM      0-1 B    operand registers
SIB        0-1 B    base + index*scale
disp       0-4 B    displacement
imm        0-8 B    immediate
```

- **REX** (`0x40`–`0x4F`) was added for 64-bit mode: its W bit selects 64-bit operands and three more bits extend register numbers from 3 bits (8 registers) to 4 bits (16 registers), by the same doubling rule as the A64 register fields.
- **ModRM** says which register and which memory or register operand: `mod` (2 bits), `reg` (3), `rm` (3).
- **SIB** (scale, index, base) describes a base register plus an index register multiplied by a scale (see the effective-address formula below).
- **disp** and **imm** are a displacement and an immediate constant.

Some real encodings:

| Instruction | Bytes |
|---|---|
| `ret` | `c3` |
| `push rbp` | `55` |
| `add rax, rdi` | `48 01 f8` |
| `mov eax, 1` | `b8 01 00 00 00` |
| `mov dword ptr [rax+rbx*4+16], 5` | `c7 44 98 10 05 00 00 00` |
| `movabs rax, 0x1122334455667788` | `48 b8` + 8 bytes |

### Decoding `48 01 f8` by hand

```
48  REX: 0100 W=1 R=0 X=0 B=0
    W=1 -> 64-bit operand size
01  opcode: ADD r/m64, r64
f8  ModRM: 11 111 000
    mod=11 -> rm is a register
    reg=111 -> rdi (source)
    rm =000 -> rax (destination)
=> add rax, rdi
```

Note that x86 arithmetic is mostly **two-operand**: `add rax, rdi` means add RDI into RAX, destroying the old `rax`. ARM64 is **three-operand**: `add x0, x1, x2` leaves both distinct source registers intact. x86 also has three-operand instruction families, including AVX and APX forms; do not generalize the legacy ADD syntax to the whole ISA.

### Why variable length hurts and helps

- It helps **code density**: short encodings can reduce instruction-cache footprint; actual code density depends on the instruction mix.
- It hurts **instruction decoding**: the decoder cannot know where the next instruction starts until it has worked out the length of the current one. Boundary detection adds work, although predecoding and parallel candidate decoding can help. Some x86 cores cache decoded **micro-ops**; this is not an ISA requirement or a universal core feature.

RISC ISAs claw back density with compressed formats: ARM's 16/32-bit Thumb-2 (on 32-bit ARM) and RISC-V's "C" extension of 16-bit instructions.

## Key takeaways
- Legacy x86 encodings combine optional prefixes and operand fields.
- Decode ModRM together with REX and the opcode.
- Variable length can improve density while adding boundary-detection work.

options.explanation: This swaps source and destination. With opcode `01` the `rm` field (011 = rbx) is the destination and `reg` (000 = rax) is the source.

questions.prompt: Why does finding several instruction boundaries in a fetch block require extra work for variable-length x86 encodings compared with fixed-width A64?

options.text: x86 instructions are 1–15 bytes long, so the start of each instruction is unknown until the previous one's length has been worked out
options.explanation: Fixed-width A64 boundaries follow at four-byte intervals from an aligned instruction start. x86 length depends on instruction fields, so parallel decoding needs boundary detection or precomputed boundary information. Particular cores may use decoded-instruction caches.

options.text: x86 has more registers to decode
options.explanation: Register count does not explain variable instruction boundaries. Baseline x86-64 has 16 general-purpose registers; APX extends it to 32.

options.text: x86 instructions must be translated to ARM instructions first
options.explanation: Many high-performance x86 cores decode to their own internal micro-ops, not to ARM. And translation happens *after* the boundary-finding problem.

options.text: x86 is little-endian, which makes byte order harder to decode
options.explanation: The central issue is variable instruction length, not data endianness. A64 instruction encoding has its own fixed byte-order rules independent of configurable data endianness.

questions.workedExample: A 32-byte block beginning on an A64 instruction boundary contains eight complete A64 instructions. An x86 block can contain varying numbers of complete instructions plus partial ones. Hardware can use length detection, predecode metadata or speculative candidate decoding; decoded-instruction caches can avoid some repeated work. This does not make a wide A64 decoder effortless.

lessons.title: Addressing modes, pointer updates and LEA
lessons.summary: Trace scaled addresses, post-indexed loads and arithmetic using LEA.
lessons.body:
The examples use Intel syntax for x86-64 and A64 syntax for AArch64. Register contents and byte-sized element widths are stated for each address calculation.

## Addressing modes

An **addressing mode** is a rule for where an operand comes from. Here are the common ones, with `x86-64` and `ARM64` examples:

| Mode | x86-64 | ARM64 |
|---|---|---|
| Immediate | `mov eax, 5` | `mov w0, #5` |
| Register | `mov rax, rdi` | `mov x0, x1` |
| Register indirect | `[rdi]` | `[x0]` |
| Base + displacement | `[rdi + 8]` | `[x0, #8]` |
| Base + scaled index | `[rdi + rsi*4]` | `[x0, x1, lsl #2]` |
| PC-relative | `[rip + label]` | `adr`, `adrp`, literal `ldr` |
| General load/store pre-/post-index | no general bracket form; string/stack instructions can update pointers implicitly | `[x0, #8]!` / `[x0], #8` |

The **effective address** is the address the mode computes. The most general x86 memory operand adds a base, a scaled index and a displacement. Take this operand with `rdi = 0x1000` and `rsi = 3`:

```
[rdi + rsi*4 + 8]
```

```formula
EA = base + index × scale + disp
EA = 0x1000 + 3 × 4 + 8
EA = 0x1000 + 20 = 0x1014
where
EA: the effective address: the memory address the instruction actually reads or writes
base: the value in the base register, here rdi = 0x1000 (hexadecimal, 4096 in decimal)
index: the value in the index register, here rsi = 3
scale: a constant multiplier written into the instruction: 1, 2, 4 or 8 on x86; here 4, the size of an `int`
disp: the displacement: a constant offset in bytes written into the instruction, here 8
In words: start at the base address, step over index elements of scale bytes each, then add a fixed offset; 20 in decimal is 0x14, giving 0x1014.
```

Each part is optional: drop the index for base + displacement, drop the displacement for base + scaled index.

What each mode is for:

- **Base + displacement**: struct fields (`p->next` could be `[p + 8]` for a layout with that field offset) and stack slots (`[rsp + 24]`).
- **Scaled index**: arrays. Scales are 1, 2, 4 or 8 on x86, matching element sizes.
- **PC-relative**: globals and constants, so code works wherever it is loaded (position-independent code, covered in the later linking units). Its reach is limited by the signed offset field; the next unit develops the reach formulas.
- **Pre/post-index**: ARM64 updates the base register as a side effect. `ldr w9, [x0], #4` loads `*x0` then adds 4 to `x0`: a pointer walk in one instruction. With `[x0, #-16]!`, the base is updated first, which is how ARM64 pushes onto the stack.

> [!tip] `lea` is the address calculator
> x86's `lea` (load effective address) computes the address and puts it in a register *without touching memory*. Compilers use it as a shift-and-add that preserves flags (it still consumes execution resources): `lea rax, [rdi + rdi*4 + 7]` multiplies by 5 and adds 7 in one instruction, as the formula below shows.

```formula
rax = x + x × 4 + 7
rax = 5x + 7
where
rax: the destination register, which receives the computed number
x: the input value held in register rdi
In words: the address arithmetic adds x to four times x, then 7, so with x = 10 the result is 57, and no memory is read.
```

These formulas describe values that fit the destination. At machine width, LEA and integer arithmetic keep the permitted low bits; the 32-bit LEA form also clears the upper half of its destination register.

## Key takeaways
- Effective addresses combine a base, scaled index and displacement.
- AArch64 pre/post-index forms update their base register.
- LEA computes address arithmetic without loading memory or changing flags.

RBX holds address 0x2000 and RCX holds index 5. What is the effective address of this x86-64 operand?

options.explanation: This adds 5 and 16 without scaling the index. The index is multiplied by the scale (8) first.
Correct. 5 × 8 = 40 = 0x28, plus 16 = 0x10 gives 0x38; add the base 0x2000 to get 0x2038.
This treats 5 × 8 = 40 as if it were 0x40. It is 40 in *decimal*, which is 0x28; plus 0x10 gives 0x38, not 0x50.

options.text: The value stored at address 0x2000
options.explanation: That would be `[rbx]` alone. And the question asks for the *address* the operand computes, not the value loaded from it.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
EA = base + index × scale + disp
EA = 0x2000 + 5 × 8 + 16
EA = 0x2000 + 56 = 0x2038
where
EA: the effective address: the memory address the operand points at
base: the value in the base register, here rbx = 0x2000 (0x marks hexadecimal)
index: the value in the index register, here rcx = 5
scale: the multiplier in the operand, here 8
disp: the displacement: a constant byte offset in the operand, here 16
In words: start at the base, step over 5 elements of 8 bytes, then add 16 more bytes; 40 + 16 = 56 in decimal is 0x38.
```

questions.prompt:
Memory holds the 32-bit values `7` at address 0x1000 and `9` at 0x1004. With `x0 = 0x1000`, this runs:

```
ldr  w1, [x0], #4
ldr  w2, [x0]
```

What are `w1`, `w2` and `x0` afterwards?

options.explanation: That is the **pre-index** behaviour (`[x0, #4]!`), which updates x0 before loading. The form `[x0], #4` is post-index: it loads first.
This ignores the write-back. The `, #4` after the brackets adds 4 to x0 after the load.
Correct. Post-index loads from the old x0 (0x1000, value 7), then sets x0 = 0x1004. The second load reads 0x1004, value 9.
Only the first instruction writes back. `ldr w2, [x0]` has no index update, so x0 stays 0x1004.

questions.workedExample:
```
start         x0 = 0x1000
ldr w1,[x0],#4
  load [0x1000] -> w1 = 7
  then x0 += 4  -> x0 = 0x1004
ldr w2,[x0]
  load [0x1004] -> w2 = 9
```

Post-index (`[x0], #4`) = use then bump: a pointer walk like `*p++`. Pre-index (`[x0, #4]!`) = bump then use, like `*++p`; it is how `stp x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!` pushes onto the stack.

questions.prompt:
With RDI initially holding 7, what does this x86-64 instruction do?

```
lea  eax, [rdi + rdi*2]
```

options.text: Loads the 32-bit value stored at address 21 into eax
options.explanation: `lea` never accesses memory. It computes the address expression and stores the *address itself*. A `mov eax, [rdi + rdi*2]` would load from memory.

options.text: Sets EAX to 14, because the scale only applies to the base register
options.explanation: The scale applies to the *index* (the second rdi), so it is 7 + 14 = 21.

options.text: Faults, because the same register cannot be both base and index
options.explanation: Using the same register as base and index is perfectly legal; it is the standard trick for multiplying by 3, 5 or 9.

options.text: Sets EAX to 21, without touching memory or the flags
options.explanation: Correct. lea computes 7 + 7 × 2 = 21. Compilers use it as a cheap multiply-and-add that doesn't disturb the flags.

questions.workedExample:
1. `lea` = load effective address. It runs the address calculation and writes the result, with no memory access.
2. Work out the address expression:

```formula
EA = base + index × scale
EA = 7 + 7 × 2 = 21
where
EA: the effective address that lea computes and writes into eax
base: the base register, rdi = 7
index: the index register, also rdi = 7
scale: the multiplier, 2
In words: 7 plus twice 7 is 21, written to eax without reading memory.
```

3. So eax = 21, three times the input.
4. Using the same register as base and index gives a cheap multiply:

```formula
r = x + x × s = (1 + s) × x
where
r: the result lea writes
x: the input value, used as both base and index
s: the scale, 2, 4 or 8
In words: scales of 2, 4 and 8 multiply by 3, 5 and 9 in one instruction; an optional displacement adds a constant, so `lea rax, [rdi + rdi*4 + 7]` gives 5 × x + 7.
```

lessons.title: How far PC-relative instructions reach
lessons.summary: Calculate the reference point and reach of RIP-relative and ADRP addressing.
lessons.body:
How far can a PC-relative offset reach? A signed field of k bits (two's complement) holds half its patterns as negatives:

```formula
−2^{k−1} ≤ d ≤ 2^{k−1} − 1
where
d: the signed offset stored in the instruction
k: the width of the offset field, in bits
≤: less than or equal to
In words: a signed k-bit field runs from minus 2 to the power (k − 1) up to one less than plus that amount; the positive side is one short because zero takes one of the non-negative patterns.
```

A normal x86-64 RIP-relative operand has a 32-bit displacement (disp32), measured from the next instruction:

```formula
target = rip_next + d
−2^31 ≤ d ≤ 2^31 − 1
2^31 B = 2 GiB
where
target: the address being referred to
rip_next: the address of the instruction after this one (x86-64's instruction pointer, RIP, after the fetch)
d: the signed 32-bit displacement, in bytes
B: byte
GiB: gibibyte: 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 bytes
≤: less than or equal to
In words: a RIP-relative operand reaches from 2 GiB before the next instruction to 1 byte short of 2 GiB after it.
```

AArch64 `adrp` counts in 4 KiB pages from the current PC rounded down to a 4 KiB boundary:

```formula
PC_page = PC − (PC mod 4096)
target = PC_page + imm21 × 4096
−2^20 ≤ imm21 ≤ 2^20 − 1
where
PC_page: the address of the adrp instruction rounded down to a multiple of 4096
PC: the address of the adrp instruction itself
mod: modulo: the remainder after division, so PC mod 4096 is how far PC sits past a 4 KiB boundary
target: the start of the 4 KiB page being referred to
imm21: the signed 21-bit offset in the instruction, counted in 4 KiB units
4096: 4 KiB (kibibytes) = 4096 bytes, the unit adrp counts in
≤: less than or equal to
In words: adrp reaches about a million (1,048,576) 4 KiB pages either side of the current page, from 4 GiB below it to 4 KiB short of 4 GiB above it; a following instruction adds the low 12 bits of the exact address.
```

These are encoding units, not a requirement that the OS use 4 KiB pages.

## Key takeaways
- Signed offsets have an asymmetric negative and positive range.
- RIP-relative displacement starts from the next instruction.
- ADRP uses four-kibibyte encoding units, independently of the OS page size.

lessons.title: Instruction count is only one performance factor
lessons.summary: Use the performance equation to compare instruction counts and clock costs.
lessons.body:
## Who won?

Neither, really. The battle lines blurred:

- Many high-performance x86 cores decode instructions into internal **micro-ops** and execute them out of order. Neither out-of-order execution nor any particular micro-op format is mandated by x86; some x86 implementations are in-order.
- RISC ISAs grew complex instructions where they pay off: ARM64 has load/store pair (`ldp`/`stp`), atomic read-modify-write instructions, and SIMD and vector extensions.

Encoding, available operations, memory-ordering rules and compatibility requirements remain important differences. Do not infer a whole chip’s power consumption or performance from “RISC” or “CISC” alone.

A detailed account of market-share causes and a universal quantitative decoder-power comparison are omitted: these require evidence about particular products, workloads and periods, beyond the architectural contracts reviewed here.

## Pitfalls

- **"CISC is slower."** Instruction count is not speed. What matters is total run time, which the next module's iron law splits into three factors:

```formula
T = N CPI t_clk
where
T: the time the program takes to run, in seconds (s)
N: the number of instructions executed
CPI: cycles per instruction: the average number of clock cycles each instruction takes
t_clk: the clock period: the length of one clock cycle, in seconds; 1 nanosecond at 1 GHz
In words: run time is how many instructions run, times how many cycles each takes on average, times how long a cycle lasts.
```

At the same clock, 1 million instructions at an average of 2 cycles each take exactly as long as 2 million at 1 cycle each. Both styles have world-class implementations.
- **Counting instructions, not bytes.** Three ARM64 instructions can be the same size as one long x86 instruction.
- **Assuming any constant fits.** The A64 immediate ADD form accepts 0–4095, optionally shifted left 12. Other constants need a different sequence.
- **Forgetting x86 is two-operand.** `sub rax, rdi` subtracts RDI from RAX and overwrites RAX; reading it as three-operand gets the direction wrong.

## Key takeaways
- Instruction count, average cycles and clock period jointly determine run time.
- Internal micro-ops and out-of-order execution are implementation choices.
- Compare byte counts and actual workloads instead of predicting speed from ISA labels.
