Because the clock period is identical in the stated model, elapsed execution time is also identical. Real comparisons must measure the relevant counts and costs.

questions.prompt: Which statements about RISC and CISC **today** are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Many high-performance x86 cores decode instructions into internal micro-ops and execute out of order
options.explanation: Correct for many implementations; it is not mandated by the ISA and does not describe every x86 core.

options.text: ARM64 includes instructions that load or store two registers at once (`ldp`/`stp`)
options.explanation: Correct. These are not strictly 'one simple operation', showing RISC ISAs adopt more complex instructions when they pay off (here: saving and restoring register pairs in prologues).

options.text: ARM64 code mixes 16-bit and 32-bit instructions to improve code density
options.explanation: That's Thumb-2, which belongs to 32-bit ARM (AArch32). A64 instructions are always 32 bits. RISC-V's C extension is the 64-bit-era example of mixing lengths.

options.text: Variable-length encodings can improve code density for suitable instruction mixes, while requiring boundary detection
options.explanation: Correct as a trade-off, not a promise that every x86 program is smaller than its A64 equivalent.

options.text: CISC processors are inherently slower because they execute more complex instructions
options.explanation: Run time depends on instruction count, cycles per instruction (CPI) and clock period multiplied together (the iron law in the worked example), and both families have top-performing implementations. 'Inherently slower' is the old 1980s argument, not today's reality.

questions.workedExample:
The first, second and fourth statements are true with their stated qualifications. A64 is fixed at 32 bits; Thumb-2 and RISC-V compressed extensions illustrate mixed instruction lengths. Microarchitecture and workload determine performance, not the RISC/CISC label alone:

```formula
T = N × CPI × t_clk
where
T: the program's run time, in seconds
N: the number of instructions executed
CPI: average clock cycles per instruction
t_clk: the clock period: the length of one clock cycle, in seconds
In words: complex instructions can lower N but raise CPI; what counts is the product.
```

lessons.title: Register names, views and zero extension
lessons.summary: Read x86 and AArch64 register names and track writes at different widths.
lessons.body:
Very few engineers write assembly. Many more need to **read** it: a crash in a release build with no debug symbols, a `perf` profile pointing at one hot loop, checking whether the compiler vectorised something, or reverse engineering a binary. The goal of this lesson is to make compiler output readable, not to make you an assembly programmer.

The best way to practise is [Compiler Explorer](https://godbolt.org/): type C on the left, see assembly for any compiler and target on the right, with colour-matched lines.

## The registers

### x86-64

Baseline x86-64 provides sixteen 64-bit general-purpose registers; APX adds more on supporting implementations. The first eight have historical names; the 64-bit extension added `r8` to `r15`. Each can be used at smaller widths:

| 64-bit | 32 | 16 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rax` | `eax` | `ax` | `al` |
| `rdi` | `edi` | `di` | `dil` |
| `rsp` | `esp` | `sp` | `spl` |
| `r8` | `r8d` | `r8w` | `r8b` |

The others follow the same pattern: `rbx`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `rsi`, `rbp`, `r9`–`r15`. `rsp` is the stack pointer. `rip` is the instruction pointer. `rflags` holds condition flags.

> [!warning] The 32-bit write rule
> Writing a 32-bit register **zeroes the upper 32 bits** of the 64-bit register. `mov eax, -1` leaves RAX holding 0x00000000ffffffff. Writing an 8- or 16-bit register leaves the other bits **unchanged**. Compilers lean on the first rule constantly: `mov eax, edi` is how they zero-extend a 32-bit value to 64 bits.

Why does −1 become `0xffffffff`? In two's complement, a negative 32-bit value is stored as the unsigned pattern 4,294,967,296 higher (one more than the largest 32-bit number):

```formula
u = v + 2^32   for v < 0
u = −1 + 4294967296 = 4294967295
u = 0xffffffff
where
u: the unsigned number formed by the 32 stored bits
v: the signed value written, here −1
2^32: 4,294,967,296, the number of different 32-bit patterns
<: less than
In words: −1 in 32 bits is the all-ones pattern, 0xffffffff in hexadecimal; writing it to eax clears the top half of rax, so rax holds 4,294,967,295, not −1.
```

### ARM64

Thirty-one 64-bit registers `x0` to `x30`, each with a 32-bit view `w0` to `w30`. Writing a `w` register zeroes the upper 32 bits, like x86.

- `x29` is the frame pointer and `x30` the **link register** (return address).
- Register number 31 is either `sp` (stack pointer) or `xzr`/`wzr`, a **zero register** that reads as 0 and discards writes. Which one depends on the instruction.
- The PC is not a general register; you reach it through `adr` and branch instructions.
- Flags live in `NZCV`: Negative, Zero, Carry, oVerflow.

## Key takeaways
- A 32-bit register write clears the upper half on both ISAs.
- x86 byte and sixteen-bit writes preserve the remaining bits.
- AArch64 register encoding 31 is instruction-dependent: stack pointer or zero.

## Further reading
- [Compiler Explorer](https://godbolt.org/)
- [x86 and amd64 instruction reference — Félix Cloutier](https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/)
- [x86-64 machine-level programming — CMU handout (PDF)](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~fp/courses/15213-s07/misc/asm64-handout.pdf)
- [X86-64 — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X86-64)
- [AArch64 — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AArch64)
- [FLAGS register — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FLAGS_register)

questions.prompt:
`rax` holds `0xffffffffffffffff`. This x86-64 instruction runs:

```
mov  eax, 0x12345678
```

What is `rax` now?

options.text: `0xffffffff12345678`
options.explanation: This assumes the upper half is preserved, which is what happens for 8- and 16-bit writes. A 32-bit write is different: it zeroes the upper 32 bits.
Correct. In 64-bit mode an ordinary write to EAX clears RAX’s upper half, leaving the specified zero-extended value.
Registers are not replicated. The upper 32 bits are simply cleared.

options.text: `0x12345678ffffffff`
options.explanation: `eax` is the *low* 32 bits of `rax`, not the high 32 bits.

questions.workedExample:
1. `eax` names bits 31–0 of `rax`.
2. Rule: a write to a 32-bit register zero-extends to 64 bits.
3. So bits 63–32 become 0 and bits 31–0 become 0x12345678.
4. Contrast: `mov ax, 0x5678` would leave bits 63–16 untouched, giving `0xffffffffffff5678`.

ARM64 behaves the same way: writing `w0` clears the top half of `x0`.

questions.prompt: `rax` starts as `0xffffffffffffffff`. Which single instructions leave **all 64 bits** of `rax` equal to zero? Select all that apply.

options.text: `xor eax, eax`
options.explanation: Correct. XOR clears EAX and its 32-bit write clears the upper half of RAX. The two-byte zero idiom is also recognized as independent of the old register value on many cores.

options.text: `mov al, 0`
options.explanation: Writing an 8-bit register leaves bits 63–8 unchanged, giving 0xffffffffffffff00.

options.text: `mov eax, 0`
options.explanation: Correct. Same 32-bit zero-extension rule; it's just a longer encoding (5 bytes) than `xor eax, eax`.

options.text: `mov ax, 0`
options.explanation: 16-bit writes also preserve the upper bits: the result is 0xffffffffffff0000.

options.text: `sub rax, rax`
options.explanation: Correct. rax - rax = 0 in full 64 bits. It works, though `xor eax, eax` is the preferred idiom.

questions.workedExample:
Apply the width rule to each:

```
xor eax,eax  32-bit write -> rax = 0
mov al,0     8-bit  -> ...ffffff00
mov eax,0    32-bit write -> rax = 0
mov ax,0     16-bit -> ...ffff0000
sub rax,rax  64-bit -> rax = 0
```

32- and 64-bit writes define every bit of rax; 8- and 16-bit writes merge into the old value.

lessons.title: Read Intel, AT&T and A64 syntax
lessons.summary: Translate operand order and recognise the main instruction families.
lessons.body:
## Syntax: three dialects

You will meet Intel syntax, AT&T syntax and ARM syntax. Here is a representative implementation of `long f(long x) { return x * 5 + 7; }`, assuming 64-bit `long`, the System V x86-64 or AAPCS64 integer convention, and inputs without signed overflow:

```
# x86-64, Intel syntax (GCC/Clang)
f:
    lea   rax, [rdi + rdi*4 + 7]
    ret
```

```
# x86-64, AT&T syntax (GDB, objdump)
f:
    leaq  7(%rdi,%rdi,4), %rax
    ret
```

```
// ARM64
f:
    add   x8, x0, x0, lsl #2   // x8 = x*5
    add   x0, x8, #7
    ret
```

| | Intel | AT&T |
|---|---|---|
| Operand order | `dst, src` | `src, dst` |
| Registers | `rax` | `%rax` |
| Constants | `7` | `$7` |
| Memory | `[b + i*s + d]` | `d(b,i,s)` |
| Size | `qword ptr` | suffix `q`, `l`, `w`, `b` |

Both memory spellings describe the same effective address:

```formula
EA = b + i × s + d
where
EA: the effective address: the memory address the operand points at
b: the value in the base register
i: the value in the index register
s: the scale: 1, 2, 4 or 8
d: the displacement: a constant byte offset
In words: Intel writes [b + i*s + d] and AT&T writes d(b,i,s); both mean base plus scaled index plus offset, so AT&T's 7(%rdi,%rdi,4) is rdi + rdi × 4 + 7.
```

All three listings compute the same number. The ARM64 version builds five times x from a shift: `lsl #2` (logical shift left by 2 bits) multiplies by 4.

```formula
x8 = x0 + x0 × 2^2 = 5 × x0
x0_out = 5x0 + 7
x0_out = 5 × 10 + 7 = 57
where
x0: the argument x, which arrives in register x0
x8: a scratch register holding 5 × x
x0_out: the return value, written back into x0
2^2: 4: shifting left by 2 bits multiplies by 4
In words: x plus four times x is five times x; add 7 and return it, so f(10) is 57.
```

GNU GDB and GNU `objdump` normally default to AT&T on x86; `objdump -d -M intel` and GDB's `set disassembly-flavor intel` switch. This module uses Intel syntax with GNU assembler conventions (`#` comments) for x86, and standard syntax with `//` comments for ARM64. A64 instructions with an explicit result normally put the destination first; stores such as `str w0, [x1]` put the source register before the destination address.

## The core instructions

| Job | x86-64 | ARM64 |
|---|---|---|
| Copy | `mov` | `mov` |
| Load / store | `mov` with `[...]` | `LDR` / `STR` |
| Address arithmetic | `lea` | `add`, `adr`, `adrp` |
| Arithmetic | `add sub imul neg` | `add sub mul neg` |
| Bitwise | `and or xor not shl shr sar` | `and orr eor mvn lsl lsr asr` |
| Compare | `cmp`, `test` | `cmp`, `tst` |
| Branch | `jmp`, `jcc` | `b`, `b.cond`, `cbz`, `cbnz` |
| Call / return | `call`, `ret` | `bl`, `ret` |
| Conditional select | `cmovcc`, `setcc` | `csel`, `cset`, `cinc` |

## Practical reading tips

- **Compile at `-O1` or `-O2` to learn.** `-O0` output often stores locals to the stack and reloads them, which is accurate but noisy.
- **Start at the end.** For a simple integer result, look for `rax`/`x0` before `ret`; other return types follow different ABI rules.
- **Map arguments first.** For ordinary fixed-parameter integer/pointer arguments under the conventions shown: `rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9` on x86-64 and `x0`–`x7` on ARM64.
- **Look for backward branches** to find loops, and **scaled addressing** to find array indexing.
- **Use the tools.** `objdump -d -M intel prog`, GDB's `disassemble` and `layout asm`, `perf annotate` for hot instructions.

## Key takeaways
- Intel syntax writes destination first; AT&T reverses ordinary two-operand order.
- The same address arithmetic has different bracket/parenthesis notation.
- Stores on A64 list the source register before its destination address.

## Further reading
- [Compiler Explorer](https://godbolt.org/)
- [x86 and amd64 instruction reference — Félix Cloutier](https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/)
- [x86-64 machine-level programming — CMU handout (PDF)](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~fp/courses/15213-s07/misc/asm64-handout.pdf)
- [X86-64 — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X86-64)
- [AArch64 — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AArch64)
- [FLAGS register — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FLAGS_register)

questions.prompt:
GDB shows this AT&T-syntax instruction:

```
subq  %rdi, %rax
```

What does it compute?

options.text: Subtract RAX from RDI, storing in RDI
options.explanation: That reads it in Intel order (destination first). In AT&T syntax the destination is the *last* operand, `%rax`.

options.text: Subtract RAX from RDI, storing in RAX
options.explanation: The destination is right, but the subtraction is reversed. AT&T `sub src, dst` means subtract the source from the destination and overwrite the destination.

options.text: Subtract RDI from RAX, storing in RAX
options.explanation: Correct. AT&T is `op src, dst`, so this is `rax -= rdi`. In Intel syntax it would be written `sub rax, rdi`.

options.text: It compares `rdi` and `rax` without storing a result
options.explanation: That would be `cmpq`. `subq` stores the difference (and also sets the flags).

questions.workedExample:
1. Spot the dialect: `%` on registers and the `q` size suffix mean AT&T.
2. AT&T order is source first, destination last.
3. So the destination is `%rax`, the source is `%rdi`, and `sub` means destination minus source.
4. Result: subtract RDI from RAX and retain the result in RAX. In Intel syntax: `sub rax, rdi`.

questions.prompt:
What does this function return for an input of 7?

```
# long times(long x)
times:
    lea   rax, [rdi + rdi*2]
    shl   rax, 2
    ret
```

options.explanation: That is only the `lea` step (7 + 7 × 2). The `shl rax, 2` then multiplies by 4.
This applies the shift to the original x (7 × 4). The shift applies to rax, which already holds 3x.
Shift left by 2 multiplies by 4, not by 8; `shl rax, 3` would multiply by 8.
Correct. `lea` computes 7 + 14 = 21 (x × 3), then shifting left by 2 multiplies by 4: 21 × 4 = 84, i.e. x × 12.

questions.workedExample:
```
rdi = 7
lea rax,[rdi+rdi*2]  rax = 7 + 14 = 21
shl rax, 2           rax = 21 * 4 = 84
```

As one formula:

```formula
r = (x + x × 2) × 2^2 = 12 × x
r = (7 + 14) × 4 = 84
where
r: the value returned in rax
x: the argument, which arrives in rdi (here 7)
2^2: 4: `shl rax, 2` shifts left by 2 bits, which multiplies by 4
In words: lea makes three times x, the shift makes that four times bigger, so the function multiplies by 12.
```

So the function is `x * 12`. Compilers replace `imul` by small constants with `lea` and shifts when their cost model favors it. Recognising `lea` with a scale as 'multiply by 3, 5 or 9' is one of the most useful reading skills.

lessons.title: Flags, signed comparisons and conditional operations
lessons.summary: Choose condition codes and trace fixed-width comparison and conditional-negation behaviour.
lessons.body:
## Flags and conditional branches

Flag-based branches such as x86 `jcc` and A64 `b.cond` read flags set by an earlier instruction. Other branches test a register directly, such as A64 `cbz`/`cbnz` and `tbz`/`tbnz`.

- For same-width operands called first and second, Intel/A64 `cmp` sets flags as if subtracting the second from the first, without retaining the subtraction result.
- `test a, b` computes `a & b`, sets flags and throws the result away. `test rax, rax` is the idiomatic "is rax zero or negative?" check.
- Ordinary arithmetic (`add`, `sub`, `and`) sets flags too on x86. On ARM64 ordinary ADD/SUB/AND leave flags unchanged unless using the flag-setting forms: `adds`, `subs`, `ands`, plus `cmp` and `tst`.

Call the first compared value **a** and the second **b**, with the same operand width. After the comparison, choose the branch by **signedness**:

| Meaning | x86 signed / unsigned | ARM64 signed / unsigned |
|---|---|---|
| first greater than second | `jg` / `ja` | `b.gt` / `b.hi` |
| first greater than or equal | `jge` / `jae` | `b.ge` / `b.hs` |
| first less than second | `jl` / `jb` | `b.lt` / `b.lo` |
| first less than or equal | `jle` / `jbe` | `b.le` / `b.ls` |
| equal | `je` | `b.eq` |

For these same-width integer comparisons, signedness determines which condition code interprets the flags. It can also affect earlier conversions and instruction selection. The bits in the register are the same; `jg` tests the sign, overflow and zero flags, while `ja` tests the carry and zero flags.

AArch64 conditional operations also read these flags: `cneg w0, w0, lt` negates the low 32-bit value only when the signed less-than condition holds. It operates on fixed-width bits; negating the smallest signed value still leaves its two’s-complement bit pattern. A C absolute-value function needs a representable-result precondition.

## Pitfalls

- **Mixing up AT&T and Intel order.** `sub %rdi, %rax` is `rax -= rdi`. Check for `%` signs before reading.
- **Reading `cmp` backwards.** In Intel x86 syntax and A64 syntax, `cmp a, b` then "greater than" means `a > b`.
- **Assuming flags survive.** On x86 nearly every arithmetic instruction overwrites them; `mov` and `lea` do not, which is one reason compilers like `lea`.
- **Treating `inc` like `add 1`.** On x86, `inc` leaves the carry flag unchanged.
- **Forgetting zero-extension.** `mov eax, ...` silently clears the top of `rax`; `mov al, ...` does not.

## Key takeaways
- CMP records a subtraction’s flags without keeping the result.
- Signed and unsigned branches interpret those flags differently.
- A flag-changing instruction between comparison and branch changes the tested condition.

## Further reading
- [Compiler Explorer](https://godbolt.org/)
- [x86 and amd64 instruction reference — Félix Cloutier](https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/)
- [x86-64 machine-level programming — CMU handout (PDF)](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~fp/courses/15213-s07/misc/asm64-handout.pdf)
- [X86-64 — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X86-64)
- [AArch64 — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AArch64)
- [FLAGS register — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FLAGS_register)

questions.prompt:
What C condition does this x86-64 pair implement?

```
test  rdi, rdi
je    .Lnull
```

options.text: `if (rdi == rdi) goto Lnull;`, so it always jumps
options.explanation: `test` is a bitwise AND, not a comparison of the two operands for equality. ZF is set only when the AND result is zero.

options.text: `if (rdi != 0) goto Lnull;`
options.explanation: That would be `jne`. `je` jumps when ZF is set, which happens when rdi is zero.

options.text: `if (rdi < 0) goto Lnull;`
options.explanation: A sign check would use `js` (jump if sign) or `jl` after the test. `je` tests the zero flag.

options.text: `if (rdi == 0) goto Lnull;`
options.explanation: Correct. `test rdi, rdi` computes rdi AND rdi (which is just rdi) and sets ZF if it is zero; `je` (jump if equal, i.e. ZF set) branches. It is the standard null-pointer or zero check.

questions.workedExample:
1. `test a, b` computes `a & b`, sets the flags, discards the result.
2. `rdi & rdi = rdi`, so ZF = 1 exactly when rdi is 0.
3. `je` is the same as `jz`: jump if ZF = 1.
4. So: if rdi is zero (for example a NULL pointer), jump to `.Lnull`.

Compilers prefer `test rdi, rdi` over `cmp rdi, 0` because it encodes shorter and does the same job.

questions.prompt:
`edi = -1` and `esi = 1`. Is the branch taken?

```
cmp   edi, esi
ja    .Lbig
```

options.text: No, because -1 is less than 1
options.explanation: That is the *signed* reading, which `jg` would use. `ja` is an unsigned condition.

options.text: Yes, because `ja` compares unsigned, and -1 is 0xffffffff, which is larger than 1
options.explanation: Correct. The register bits are 0xffffffff. `ja` (jump if above) treats both as unsigned: 4,294,967,295 > 1, so it jumps. In C this is what happens with `if ((unsigned)a > (unsigned)b)`.

options.text: No, because `ja` only works on 64-bit registers
options.explanation: `ja` reads flags; it doesn't care what width the preceding `cmp` used.

options.text: It depends on the upper 32 bits of rdi
options.explanation: `cmp edi, esi` is a 32-bit comparison; the upper bits of rdi and rsi play no part.

questions.workedExample:
1. `cmp edi, esi` computes 0xffffffff - 0x00000001 and sets flags.
2. As unsigned numbers, the 32 bits of −1 mean the largest 32-bit number:

```formula
u = v + 2^32   for v < 0
u = −1 + 4294967296 = 4294967295
u − 1 = 4294967294
where
u: the unsigned number formed by the 32 bits in edi
v: the signed value those bits represent, −1
2^32: 4,294,967,296, the number of different 32-bit patterns
<: less than
In words: read as unsigned, −1 is the largest 32-bit number, so subtracting 1 from it needs no borrow and leaves a non-zero result.
```

No borrow, so CF is clear; the result is non-zero, so ZF is clear.
3. `ja` jumps if CF is clear and ZF is clear: taken.
4. A signed `jg` would test SF, OF and ZF and see -1 < 1: not taken.

This is how a C signed/unsigned mix-up (`if (len > limit)` with an unsigned limit) becomes a security bug: a negative length looks enormous, or vice versa.

questions.prompt:
What does this ARM64 function compute? (`cneg Rd, Rn, cond` sets Rd = -Rn if the condition holds, else Rd = Rn.)

```
// int f(int x)
f:
    cmp   w0, #0
    cneg  w0, w0, lt
    ret
```

options.text: `-x` for every input
options.explanation: The negation is conditional: it happens only if the `lt` (signed less than) condition is true, that is, when x < 0.
That would be `cset w0, lt`. `cneg` returns a negated copy of the register, not a 0/1 flag.

options.text: Absolute value for inputs other than INT_MIN; for INT_MIN the 32-bit result remains 0x80000000
options.explanation: Correct. The instruction conditionally negates a 32-bit bit pattern. For ordinary inputs this gives the absolute value; INT_MIN has no positive counterpart representable as a signed 32-bit int.

options.text: `max(x, 0)`
options.explanation: max(x, 0) would return 0 for negative x. Here negatives are negated to become positive, not clamped.

questions.workedExample: CMP sets flags for x relative to zero; CNEG conditionally negates the 32-bit value. For −5, 5 and 0 the results are 5, 5 and 0. For INT_MIN the hardware result is 0x80000000, which still represents INT_MIN as signed 32-bit. This does not mean C abs(INT_MIN) is defined to wrap: that C expression has undefined behaviour when the result is unrepresentable.

lessons.title: Read a complete scalar counting loop
lessons.summary: Trace equivalent positive-count loops using indexed x86 and pointer-walking A64 code.
lessons.body:
## A worked example: counting positives

```
long count_pos(const long *a, long n) {
    long c = 0;
    for (long i = 0; i < n; i++)
        if (a[i] > 0) c++;
    return c;
}
```

The following is an illustrative scalar implementation, not a promise of exact output from any compiler version. Assume 64-bit `long` and a valid array of at least `n` elements when `n > 0`. Arguments arrive in `rdi` (`a`) and `rsi` (`n`); the result goes in `rax`. The calling-convention lesson explains why.

```
# long count_pos(const long *a, long n)
count_pos:
    xor   eax, eax         # c = 0
    test  rsi, rsi
    jle   .Ldone           # n <= 0: done
    xor   ecx, ecx         # i = 0
.Lloop:
    xor   edx, edx         # edx = 0
    cmp   qword ptr [rdi + rcx*8], 0
    setg  dl               # dl = (a[i] > 0)
    add   rax, rdx         # c += dl
    inc   rcx              # i++
    cmp   rcx, rsi
    jne   .Lloop           # i != n
.Ldone:
    ret
```

How to read it:

1. **Find the loop.** Here, the backward branch (`jne .Lloop`) forms a loop. In arbitrary code, inspect the control-flow paths rather than assuming every backward branch means a source-level loop. Everything between `.Lloop` and the branch is the body.
2. **Find the induction variable.** `rcx` starts at 0, is incremented, and is compared with `n`: that is `i`.
3. **Find the memory access.** `[rdi + rcx*8]` is `a[i]` with 8-byte elements.
4. **Notice there is no branch for the `if`.** `setg dl` turns "greater than" into a 0 or 1, and `add` adds it. The compiler replaced an unpredictable branch with arithmetic. `edx` is cleared *before* the `cmp`, because `xor` itself changes the flags.
5. **Find the return value.** `rax` is set to 0 at the top and accumulates `c`.

An equivalent A64 implementation:

```
// long count_pos(const long *a, long n)
count_pos:
    mov   x8, #0           // c = 0
    cmp   x1, #1
    b.lt  .Ldone           // n < 1: done
.Lloop:
    ldr   x9, [x0], #8     // x9 = *a++
    cmp   x9, #0
    cinc  x8, x8, gt       // if > 0: c++
    subs  x1, x1, #1       // n--, set flags
    b.ne  .Lloop
.Ldone:
    // Return the accumulated result.
    mov   x0, x8
    ret
```

The same ideas, with different instruction choices: this version rewrites `a[i]` as a pointer walk using a post-indexed load, counted `n` down to zero with `subs` (which sets the flags `b.ne` reads), and used `cinc` (conditional increment) instead of a branch.

## Key takeaways
- Find the guard, induction variable, data access and loop exit.
- SETG and CINC turn comparison results into increments.

Look again at the inner loop of the illustrative `count_pos`:

options.text: Moving `xor edx, edx` to between `cmp` and `setg` would give the same results

2. `setcc` writes one byte. The zeroing makes rdx exactly 0 or 1. True.
3. Signed vs unsigned condition codes: with `seta`, -2 (0xfff...fe) is 'above' 0. True.
4. Only `jne` is conditional; the `if` is computed arithmetically. True.

lessons.title: Zeroing, population count, division and branch-free max
lessons.summary: Recognise compiler idioms while preserving signed rounding and bounds assumptions.
lessons.body:
## Idioms that look strange at first

| You see | It means |
|---|---|
| `xor eax, eax` | EAX becomes zero (2 bytes, and many cores recognize a dependency-breaking zero idiom) |
| `test rdi, rdi` then `je` | `if (rdi == 0)` |
| `lea eax, [rdi + rdi*2]` | `eax` gets three times `rdi` (low 32 bits kept), no memory access |
| `movsxd rax, edi` / `sxtw x0, w0` | sign-extend 32 to 64 bits (an `int` to 64-bit `long` here) |
| `mov eax, edi` / `mov w0, w0` | zero-extend `unsigned` to 64 bits |
| `cmovg`, `csel` | branch-free `a > b ? a : b` |
| `nop`, `nop dword ptr [rax]` | padding to align a loop or function |
| `endbr64` / `bti c` | landing pad for control-flow protection (later hardening units) |

### Count set bits by clearing one at a time

For an unsigned fixed-width input, subtracting one flips the lowest set bit and the zero bits below it. AND with the original therefore clears exactly that lowest set bit. Repeat until zero; each successful iteration counts one set bit. An initially zero input skips the loop.

```c
// Unsigned arithmetic wraps by definition.
unsigned bits(unsigned long x) {
    unsigned count = 0;
    while (x != 0) {
        // Clear the lowest remaining bit.
        x &= x - 1;
        count++;
    }
    return count;
}
```

For input 44, the set bits are at positions two, three and five, counting from zero; three iterations return 3. This pattern explains the population-count assembly exercise without assuming a dedicated POPCNT instruction.

### Division by a constant

Division can be more expensive than a suitable multiply/shift sequence; costs depend on the instruction and core. Signed `x / 2` must round towards zero, but an arithmetic right shift rounds towards minus infinity (the machine’s arithmetic shift of −7 by one yields −4; negative signed right shift in C17 is implementation-defined). So the compiler adds 1 to negative numbers first:

```
# int half(int x) { return x / 2; }
half:
    mov   eax, edi
    shr   eax, 31        # 1 if x<0 else 0
    add   eax, edi       # bias negatives
    sar   eax, 1         # arithmetic shift
    ret
```

The arithmetic shift (`sar`) rounds down, so the bias is what turns rounding down into rounding towards zero:

```formula
q = ⌊(x + c) / 2⌋
c = 1 if x < 0, otherwise 0
q = ⌊(−7 + 1) / 2⌋ = ⌊−3⌋ = −3
⌊−7 / 2⌋ = ⌊−3.5⌋ = −4
where
q: the result the code returns, which matches C's x / 2
x: the signed integer being halved, here −7
c: the bias: 1 for a negative x, 0 otherwise; `shr eax, 31` produces it by moving the sign bit down to bit 0
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down towards minus infinity, which is what an arithmetic shift right by 1 does to a halving
<: less than
In words: without the bias −7 shifts to −4 (rounded down from −3.5); adding 1 first gives −6, which halves exactly to −3, the round-towards-zero answer C requires.
```

For a non-negative `x` the bias is 0, and rounding down already equals rounding towards zero. For non-power-of-two divisors such as 10, compilers multiply by a "magic" reciprocal constant and shift. If you see a large odd constant and an `imul` where you expected a division, division by a constant is one possibility; confirm the complete sequence before drawing that conclusion.

### Branch-free max

```
# int max(int a, int b)
max:
    mov   eax, esi       # eax = b
    cmp   edi, esi       # compare a with b
    cmovg eax, edi       # if a > b: eax = a
    ret
```

```
// int max(int a, int b)
max:
    cmp   w0, w1
    csel  w0, w0, w1, gt   // a > b ? a : b
    ret
```

## Narrow arguments need explicit widening

Under System V AMD64, a 32-bit unsigned parameter defines only its argument register’s low 32 bits; the remaining bits are unspecified. Before using that value as a 64-bit array index, use a 32-bit register write such as `mov esi, esi` to clear the upper half. A valid index and pointer do not make an uninitialised upper half safe. The ABI lesson later covers the complete argument-register sequence.

## Key takeaways
- Common short sequences implement zeroing, extension and conditional selection.
- Signed division by two needs a bias for negative odd inputs.
- Recognise candidate idioms, then confirm the full data and control flow.

## Further reading

- [X86-64 — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X86-64)

What does `mystery(44)` return? (`rdi` holds the unsigned argument; the result is in `eax`.)

```
mystery:
    # Count one bit per iteration.
    xor   eax, eax
.L1:
    test  rdi, rdi
    je    .L2
    lea   rcx, [rdi - 1]
    and   rdi, rcx
    inc   eax
    jmp   .L1
.L2:
    ret
```

options.text: 3, because it counts the 1 bits
options.explanation: Correct. `x & (x - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, so the loop runs once per 1 bit. 44 = 0b101100 has three 1 bits.

options.text: 44, because it returns its argument
options.explanation: The return value is in eax, which counts loop iterations; rdi (the argument) is destroyed by the `and`.

options.text: 6, because it counts the bits in the number
options.explanation: 44 is 6 bits long (0b101100), but the loop clears only *set* bits and stops at zero, so the zeros don't count.

options.text: 2, because it finds the position of the lowest set bit
options.explanation: The lowest set bit of 44 is indeed bit 2, but this loop doesn't stop at the first set bit; it keeps clearing bits until the value is 0.

questions.workedExample:
First write 44 in binary:

```formula
44 = 2^5 + 2^3 + 2^2 = 32 + 8 + 4
44 = 0b101100
where
2^5, 2^3, 2^2: the place values of bits 5, 3 and 2
0b: marks a binary number
In words: 44 is made of three powers of two, so its binary form has exactly three 1 bits.
```

Then trace the loop with x = 44:

```
x        x-1      x&(x-1)  eax
101100   101011   101000   1
101000   100111   100000   2
100000   011111   000000   3
000000   -> test sets ZF, je
```

Returns 3. This is Kernighan's population count: each iteration removes the lowest 1 bit. (A compiler targeting a modern CPU might just emit `popcnt` instead.)

questions.prompt:
A colleague 'optimises' the compiler's signed `x / 2` to a plain arithmetic shift after copying the argument:

```
half:              # int half(int x)
    mov   eax, edi
    sar   eax, 1
    ret
```

What does `half(-7)` now return, and is that what C's `-7 / 2` gives?

options.text: -3; same as C
options.explanation: C's `-7 / 2` is -3, but an arithmetic right shift doesn't give -3. Shifting rounds towards minus infinity.

options.text: -4; C gives -3, so the 'optimisation' is wrong for negative odd numbers
options.explanation: Correct. `sar` rounds −3.5 down to −4. C integer division truncates towards zero, giving -3. The compiler's `shr eax, 31; add eax, edi` adds 1 to negative inputs first so the shift rounds towards zero.

options.text: 2147483644; `sar` is a logical shift that fills with zeros
options.explanation: That's `shr` (logical). `sar` (arithmetic) copies the sign bit in, so negative numbers stay negative.

options.text: -3; and -4 only appears for even numbers
options.explanation: Even numbers divide exactly, so both methods agree: -8 >> 1 = -4 = -8 / 2. The mismatch is for negative *odd* numbers.

questions.workedExample:
1. -7 in 32-bit two's complement is 0xfffffff9.
2. `sar` by 1 shifts right and copies the sign bit: 0xfffffffc = -4. That is −3.5 rounded down.
3. C (since C99) truncates towards zero: -7 / 2 = -3.
4. The compiler's version adds a bias first:

```formula
q = ⌊(x + c) / 2⌋
c = 1 if x < 0, otherwise 0
q = ⌊(−7 + 1) / 2⌋ = −3
where
q: the result, matching C's x / 2
x: the signed input, here −7
c: the bias, the sign bit of x: `shr eax, 31` moves it to bit 0
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down towards minus infinity, which is what `sar` by 1 does
<: less than
In words: adding 1 to a negative input before the rounding-down shift turns it into rounding towards zero.
```

5. For positives the bias is 0, so nothing changes. (If x were `unsigned`, a plain `shr` would be right.) The shifts here describe x86 instructions; do not infer portable C17 semantics for right-shifting a negative signed integer.

questions.prompt:
A hand-written System V x86-64 function takes `(const int *table, unsigned idx)` and starts with:

```
    mov   eax, dword ptr [rdi + rsi*4]
```

It passes every test, but crashes intermittently in production when called from a larger, optimised program. What is the most likely bug? Assume idx is within the array bounds and the table pointer is valid.

options.text: It should use `rdi*4` instead of `rsi*4`
options.explanation: `rdi` holds the first argument (the pointer) and `rsi` the second (the index), so `rdi + rsi*4` is the right shape.

options.text: `dword ptr` should be `qword ptr` on a 64-bit machine
options.explanation: The elements are `int` (4 bytes), so a dword load is correct. qword would read two elements.

options.text: The ABI only defines the low 32 bits of `rsi` for an `unsigned` argument; the upper 32 bits can contain garbage, so it must zero-extend first (for example `mov esi, esi`)
options.explanation: Correct. For 32-bit arguments, the System V ABI leaves the upper half of the 64-bit register unspecified. In tests the caller happened to leave zeros there; in optimised code it may not, producing a wild address. Compilers emit `mov eax, esi` (or similar) before using such a value as a 64-bit index.

options.text: Using a scaled index is illegal with `unsigned` values
options.explanation: Scaled addressing is purely arithmetic and doesn't know about C types. The issue is what's in the upper bits of the register.

questions.workedExample:
1. The C prototype says `idx` is a 32-bit `unsigned`. The caller places it in `esi`.
2. The ABI guarantees only bits 31–0. Bits 63–32 of `rsi` are whatever the caller last left there.
3. `[rdi + rsi*4]` uses all 64 bits of `rsi`. If the top half is non-zero, the address is wildly wrong: a crash or a silent wrong read.
4. Fix: `mov esi, esi` (a 32-bit write zero-extends) or `mov eax, esi` and index with `rax`.

The lesson's `mov eax, edi` idiom table entry ('zero-extend unsigned to 64 bits') is exactly this.

lessons.title: Calls, returns and the link register
lessons.summary: Trace the different return-address mechanisms and why nested calls need saved state.
lessons.body:
A function compiled today by Clang must be callable from code compiled years ago by GCC, from Rust, from Go via cgo, or from a hand-written assembly routine. That only works if everyone agrees on the details: where the arguments go, where the result comes back, which registers a call may destroy, and how the stack is laid out.

That agreement is the **calling convention**, part of a platform's **ABI** (application binary interface). The ABI also covers type sizes, struct layout and how system calls are made. Break the convention and you get crashes that look impossible: a variable that changes "by itself" across a call, or a segfault inside `printf`.

## Call and return

The hardware mechanism differs between the two ISAs.

**x86-64** keeps the return address on the stack:

- `call f` pushes the address of the next instruction (moves `rsp` down 8 bytes, then stores it) and jumps to `f`.
- `ret` pops that address into `rip`.

```formula
rsp_call = rsp − 8
rsp_ret = rsp_call + 8 = rsp
where
rsp: the stack pointer just before the call: the address of the current top of the stack
rsp_call: the stack pointer after call has pushed the return address
rsp_ret: the stack pointer after ret has popped it again
8: a return address is 64 bits = 8 bytes
In words: the stack grows towards lower addresses, so pushing subtracts 8 and popping adds the same 8 back; if rsp was 0x1000 before the call, it is 0xff8 inside the function and 0x1000 again after the return.
```

**ARM64** keeps it in a register:

- `bl f` (branch with link) puts the return address in `x30`, the **link register**, and jumps.
- `ret` branches to the address in `x30`.

The ARM64 design makes calls to **leaf functions** (functions that call nothing) cheap: no automatic return-address stack access from `bl`/`ret` themselves; the function can still access memory. But a function making a nested call and later returning to its own caller must preserve its original return address, or the inner `bl` will overwrite it and the outer `ret` will go to the wrong place.

## Key takeaways
- An ABI lets separately compiled code agree on machine-level interfaces.
- x86 CALL saves the return address on the stack.
- A64 BL overwrites X30; a nested ordinary return needs the original address preserved.

## Further reading
- [x86 calling conventions — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X86_calling_conventions)
- [System V x86-64 psABI — GitLab](https://gitlab.com/x86-psABIs/x86-64-ABI)
- [Procedure Call Standard for the Arm 64-bit Architecture (AAPCS64)](https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/main/aapcs64/aapcs64.rst)
- [x64 calling convention — Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/build/x64-calling-convention)
- [The return of the frame pointers — Brendan Gregg](https://www.brendangregg.com/blog/2024-03-17/the-return-of-the-frame-pointers.html)
- [Call stack — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_stack)

- [Apple ARM64 ABI differences](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/writing-arm64-code-for-apple-platforms)

questions.prompt: On ARM64, where does `bl printf` put the return address?

options.text: It pushes it onto the stack, like x86 `call`
options.explanation: `bl` writes the return address to X30 rather than pushing it to the stack. This does not promise that calling and executing an arbitrary function causes no memory traffic.

options.text: In `x29`, the frame pointer
options.explanation: `x29` is the frame pointer by convention. The return address goes in the link register, which is a different register.

options.text: In `x30`, the link register
options.explanation: Correct. `bl` (branch with link) writes the address of the next instruction into `x30` (also called `lr`) and branches. `ret` later branches to `x30`.

options.text: In `x0`, alongside the first argument
options.explanation: `x0` passes the first argument and the return value. Putting the return address there would clobber the argument.

questions.workedExample:
1. `bl` = **b**ranch with **l**ink. "Link" means: remember where to come back to.
2. AAPCS64 names `x30` the link register (LR).
3. So after `bl printf`, `x30` = address of the instruction after the `bl`.
4. A consequence: a function that makes a nested call and later returns normally must preserve its original return address (usually with `stp x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!`).

questions.prompt:
This ARM64 function was hand-written. What happens when it is called?

```
f:
    // Nested call overwrites x30.
    bl    g
    add   x0, x0, #1
    ret
```

Assume g returns normally with x30 still containing the address immediately after bl g, and ignore external interruption.

options.text: It works: `ret` returns to `f`'s caller
options.explanation: `ret` branches to whatever is in `x30` *now*, and `bl g` replaced the original return address.

options.text: It crashes immediately at the `bl`
options.explanation: The `bl` itself is fine: it calls `g` normally and `g` returns to the `add`.

options.text: After `g` returns, `ret` jumps back to the `add`, so it loops forever adding 1
options.explanation: Correct. `bl g` set `x30` to the address of the `add`. Since `f` never saved its own return address, `ret` jumps to the `add` again, and again: an infinite loop.

options.text: `ret` pops a return address from the stack, which is garbage
options.explanation: ARM64 `ret` does not use the stack at all; it reads `x30`. The stack pop behaviour belongs to x86 `ret`.

questions.workedExample:
1. On entry, `x30` = return address into `f`'s caller.
2. `bl g` overwrites `x30` with the address of `add x0, x0, #1`.
3. `g` returns there. `x0` is incremented.
4. `ret` branches to `x30`, which is still the `add`.
5. So it adds 1 and returns to the `add` forever.

The fix is the standard non-leaf prologue and epilogue:
```
f:
    stp   x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!
    mov   x29, sp
    // Nested call overwrites x30.
    bl    g
    add   x0, x0, #1
    ldp   x29, x30, [sp], #16
    ret
```

lessons.title: Argument registers, stack arguments and struct returns
lessons.summary: Place ordinary arguments and aggregate results under the two platform ABIs.
lessons.body:
A calling convention fixes how values cross a function-call boundary. The following examples compare ordinary scalar System V AMD64 and base AAPCS64 calls; platform extensions need their own rules.

## Where arguments and results go

On Linux, macOS and the BSDs, x86-64 uses the **System V AMD64 ABI**. Linux AArch64 uses **AAPCS64**; Apple’s ARM64 ABI has material differences, particularly for variadic and stack arguments. The table covers common fixed scalar parameters, not every ABI type.

| | System V x86-64 | AAPCS64 |
|---|---|---|
| Integer/pointer args | `rdi rsi rdx rcx r8 r9` | `x0`–`x7` |
| Float/double args | `xmm0`–`xmm7` | `v0`–`v7` |
| Integer return | `rax` (+ `rdx`) | `x0` (+ `x1`) |
| Float return | `xmm0` | `v0` |
| Further args | on the stack | on the stack |

Integer and floating-point arguments are counted separately. For `double f(double x, int n)`, `x` arrives in `xmm0` and `n` in `edi` (on ARM64: `d0` and `w0`).

### More than six (or eight) arguments

Here is a call to an eight-argument function `g(1, 2, ..., 8)`, in a representative System V x86-64 sequence. Assume `rsp` is already 16-byte aligned at the start of this fragment:

```
    mov   edi, 1
    mov   esi, 2
    mov   edx, 3
    mov   ecx, 4
    mov   r8d, 5
    mov   r9d, 6
    push  8          # 8th arg
    push  7          # 7th arg (lowest)
    call  g
    add   rsp, 16    # caller pops args
```

Arguments 7 and 8 go on the stack, pushed in reverse so the 7th ends up at the lower address. On entry to `g`, the return address is at `[rsp]` and the stack arguments sit just above it:

```formula
A_k = rsp + 8 × (k − 6)   for k ≥ 7
A_7 = rsp + 8 × 1 = rsp + 8
A_8 = rsp + 8 × 2 = rsp + 16
where
A_k, A_7, A_8: the address of argument number k (7 and 8 here), as seen on entry to g
k: the argument's position in the call, counting from 1
rsp: the stack pointer on entry to g, which points at the return address
6: the first six integer arguments travel in registers (rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9), so the 7th is the first on the stack
8: each stack argument slot is 8 bytes
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: skip the 8-byte return address, then each later argument is a further 8 bytes up; after the call, the caller frees the two slots with `add rsp, 16` (2 × 8 bytes).
```

This assumes each stack argument fits one 8-byte slot, as these `int`s do; larger aggregates take more. On ARM64, all eight fit in `x0`–`x7`.

### Returning structs

Aggregate returns depend on ABI classification, not size alone:

- Under System V AMD64, many ordinary aggregates up to 16 bytes return in integer and/or vector registers. Unaligned fields and other classification rules can force memory return even for small aggregates; supported vector-shaped aggregates have additional exceptions.
- Under base AAPCS64, ordinary non-homogeneous composites up to 16 bytes can use `x0`/`x1`. Homogeneous floating-point aggregates of up to four members can use vector registers even when larger than 16 bytes.
- For an indirect return, the caller supplies storage. System V passes its address in `rdi`, consuming an integer argument slot, and returns that address in `rax`. AAPCS64 uses `x8`, leaving the normal argument registers available. Consult the full ABI for complex/vector types and C++ objects.

## Key takeaways
- Integer and floating-point arguments use separate allocation rules.
- Further ordinary integer arguments occupy stack slots.
- Indirect aggregate returns use RDI in System V and X8 in base AAPCS64.

## Further reading
- [x86 calling conventions — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X86_calling_conventions)
- [System V x86-64 psABI — GitLab](https://gitlab.com/x86-psABIs/x86-64-ABI)
- [Procedure Call Standard for the Arm 64-bit Architecture (AAPCS64)](https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/main/aapcs64/aapcs64.rst)
- [x64 calling convention — Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/build/x64-calling-convention)
- [The return of the frame pointers — Brendan Gregg](https://www.brendangregg.com/blog/2024-03-17/the-return-of-the-frame-pointers.html)
- [Call stack — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_stack)

- [Apple ARM64 ABI differences](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/writing-arm64-code-for-apple-platforms)

options.text: `rcx`
options.explanation: A common slip: the order is not alphabetical a-b-c-d. `rcx` is the **fourth** integer argument; it is also the first argument on Windows x64, which adds to the confusion.

options.text: `rdx`
options.explanation: Correct. The integer argument order is `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8`, `r9`, so the third argument is in `rdx`.

options.text: `rsi`
options.explanation: `rsi` holds the **second** argument, `b`.

options.text: On the stack at `[rsp + 8]`
options.explanation: These three scalar long arguments fit in integer registers. Aggregate and other special argument classes can follow different rules.

questions.workedExample:
1. Recall the System V integer argument sequence: `rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9`.
2. Count: `a` is 1st (`rdi`), `b` is 2nd (`rsi`), `c` is 3rd (`rdx`).
3. A mnemonic some people use: "**D**iane's **S**ilk **D**ress **C**osts **8**9 dollars" for di, si, dx, cx, r8, r9.

options.text: `x` in `xmm0`, `n` in `edi`, `y` in `xmm1`
options.explanation: Correct. Integer and floating-point arguments are counted separately: `n` is the first integer argument and `y` is the second floating-point argument.

options.text: `x` in `xmm0`, `n` in `esi`, `y` in `xmm2`
options.explanation: This assumes every argument uses up a slot in both register classes, as Windows x64 does. System V counts each class independently.

options.text: `x` in `rdi`, `n` in `rsi`, `y` in `rdx`
options.explanation: Doubles never go in general-purpose registers in System V when vector registers are available; they go in `xmm0`–`xmm7`.

options.text: All three on the stack, because the types are mixed

lessons.title: Caller-saved and callee-saved registers
lessons.summary: Choose a register that survives a call and understand who must restore it.
lessons.body:
A caller transfers control to a callee and expects to continue after its return. Register-preservation rules decide which values remain valid at that point.

## Who saves which registers

A call may destroy some registers and must preserve others:

- **Caller-saved** (also called volatile registers or scratch registers): the called function may overwrite them freely. If the caller needs a value in one of these after the call, the caller must save it.
- **Callee-saved** (also called non-volatile registers): the called function must restore them before returning. If it wants to use one, it saves the old value in its prologue and restores it in its epilogue.

| | System V x86-64 | AAPCS64 |
|---|---|---|
| Callee-saved | `rbx rbp r12`–`r15`, restored `rsp` | `x19`–`x28`, `x29`, `sp` |
| Caller-saved | `rax rcx rdx rsi rdi r8`–`r11` | `x0`–`x17`, `x30` |
| Vector callee-saved | none | low 64 bits of `v8`–`v15` |

Some ARM64 registers have special jobs. `x8` passes the large-struct return pointer. `x16` and `x17` are scratch registers that linker-generated stubs may overwrite. `x18` is the **platform register**, reserved on Apple platforms and Windows. Portable code should not touch it.

Why have both kinds? If every register were caller-saved, every call site would spill everything it cared about. If every register were callee-saved, every function would save registers it uses even when no caller needs them. A split lets the compiler put short-lived values in scratch registers and values live across calls in callee-saved ones.

## Key takeaways
- Caller-saved values need preservation if the caller still needs them.
- A callee restores any callee-saved registers it changes.
- A64 platform and linker-scratch registers have additional rules.

lessons.title: Trace recursive factorial stack frames
lessons.summary: Trace the recursive factorial implementations and account for each saved stack slot.
lessons.body:
## Stack frames

When a function needs stack storage, its **stack frame** is the region of stack holding its return address, saved registers, local variables, and outgoing arguments. The stack grows **downwards** (towards lower addresses) on both ISAs.

### A recursive example

```
long fact(long n) {
    return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * fact(n - 1);
}
```

Compilers may replace this recursion with a loop. The examples below deliberately retain recursion. With 64-bit signed `long`, use inputs at most 20 for a representable factorial; the original C multiplication has undefined behaviour on signed overflow. The limit comes from comparing factorials with the largest signed 64-bit value:

```formula
L_max = 2^63 − 1 ≈ 9.22 × 10^18
20! ≈ 2.43 × 10^18 < L_max
21! ≈ 5.11 × 10^19 > L_max
where
L_max: the largest value a 64-bit signed long can store; in two's complement the top bit carries the sign, so the positive range stops at 2^63 − 1
!: factorial: n! = n × (n − 1) × … × 1, so 3! = 6
n: any whole number 1 or more
…: and so on, through every whole number in between
≈: approximately equal to
<, >: less than, greater than
In words: 20 factorial still fits in a signed 64-bit integer, but 21 factorial is more than five times too big.
```

`n` must survive the recursive call, so it goes in a callee-saved register.

```
# long fact(long n)
fact:
    push  rbx          # save callee-saved
    mov   rbx, rdi     # keep n across call
    # Base case returns one.
    mov   eax, 1
    cmp   rdi, 1
    jle   .Lret        # n <= 1: return 1
    lea   rdi, [rdi - 1]
    call  fact         # rax = fact(n-1)
    imul  rax, rbx     # rax = n * rax
.Lret:
    # Restore the caller’s saved register.
    pop   rbx
    ret
```

```
// long fact(long n)
fact:
    stp   x29, x30, [sp, #-32]!
    mov   x29, sp
    str   x19, [sp, #16]   // callee-saved
    mov   x19, x0          // keep n
    mov   x0, #1
    cmp   x19, #1
    b.le  .Lret            // n <= 1
    sub   x0, x19, #1
    bl    fact             // x0 = fact(n-1)
    mul   x0, x0, x19
.Lret:
    ldr   x19, [sp, #16]
    ldp   x29, x30, [sp], #32
    ret
```

The ARM64 prologue pushes `x29` and `x30` as a pair with a pre-indexed store, sets `x29` to point at that pair (the **frame record**), then saves `x19`. The epilogue reverses it. The x86 version has no frame pointer at all, which is normal for optimised code.

Here is the x86-64 stack while `fact(1)` runs, called as `fact(3)` from `main`. `S` is `rsp` on entry to `fact(3)`:

```
addr   contents
S      return addr into main
S-8    main's rbx (saved)
S-16   return addr into fact(3)
S-24   saved rbx = 3
S-32   return addr into fact(2)
S-40   saved rbx = 2    <- rsp in fact(1)
```

For this exact x86 listing, each active level costs 16 bytes: a return address and one saved register. The A64 listing reserves 32 bytes per active level; its return address is saved inside that allocation. Neither size is an ISA-wide recursion cost.

```formula
D = 16 × L
D = 16 × 3 = 48 bytes
where
D: the stack space used by the active fact calls, in bytes
L: how many fact calls are active at once (here fact(3), fact(2) and fact(1))
16: one 8-byte return address plus one 8-byte saved rbx per call
bytes: the unit of memory size; one byte is 8 bits
In words: stack use grows in a straight line with recursion depth; the three levels above fill the 48 bytes from S + 7 down to S − 40.
```

Unbounded recursion keeps adding frames until stack resources are exhausted. Stack limits and guard arrangements depend on the OS and thread configuration; Linux can signal `SIGSEGV` on stack exhaustion. No universal 8 MB default is assumed.

## Key takeaways
- A recursive call must preserve the input needed after it returns.
- The examples restore saved registers and the return state.
- Stack use grows with active call depth; signed factorial also has a representable range.

options.text: About 8,000 levels
options.explanation: That treats 8 MiB as 8 × 1,000 × 16 bytes or similar. The real calculation gives a number about 65 times larger.

options.text: About 8.4 million levels
options.explanation: That divides by 1 byte per level. Each level costs 16 bytes, not one.

options.text: Unlimited, because `fact` is a tail call
options.explanation: `n * fact(n - 1)` multiplies *after* the call returns, so it is not a tail call; each level's frame must stay alive.

options.text: About 524,000 levels
options.explanation: Correct under the stated idealised budget: 8,388,608 bytes divided into sixteen-byte levels permits 524,288 levels. The worked example states the simplifying assumptions.

questions.workedExample:
In the stated simplified model:

```formula
L = S / f
L = (8 × 1048576 B) / (16 B) = 524288
where
L: the number of recursion levels that fit
S: the stack size limit: 8 MiB = 8 × 1,048,576 bytes = 8,388,608 bytes
f: the stack used per level: 16 bytes
B: byte
MiB: mebibyte, 2^20 = 1,048,576 bytes
In words: divide the stack size by the bytes each call uses; 8 MiB at 16 bytes per call is about 524,000 levels.
```

Actual available depth depends on other stack use, limits, guards and generated code. This hand-written instruction sequence would wrap products at machine width; C factorial overflows a signed 64-bit long above 20 and therefore has undefined behaviour. The depth exercise is not a valid large-input C factorial computation.

lessons.title: Frame pointers, call alignment and the red zone
lessons.summary: Calculate argument offsets and alignment and identify where the red zone applies.
lessons.body:
The preceding recursive factorial saved RBX with a single push before calling itself. The following examples use System V x86-64 unless a sentence explicitly names AArch64.

### The classic frame-pointer prologue

A classic frame-pointer prologue uses `rbp` as a fixed reference point. Compiler options and target rules determine which functions actually retain frame pointers:

```
# long f(long x), -O0 style
f:
    push  rbp          # save caller's rbp
    mov   rbp, rsp     # rbp = frame base
    sub   rsp, 32      # room for locals
    mov   qword ptr [rbp - 8], rdi  # x
    mov   rax, qword ptr [rbp - 8]
    leave              # rsp = rbp, pop rbp
    ret
```

When callers and callees maintain compatible frame records, saved `rbp` values form a linked list through their frames. Debuggers and profilers walk it to produce a backtrace.

## Alignment and the red zone

**Alignment.** For the ordinary calls shown, both ABIs require 16-byte stack alignment at the call boundary. System V can require stronger alignment for some stack-passed over-aligned or vector arguments. On x86-64, `rsp` must be a multiple of 16 just *before* the `call`, so on entry to a function (after the 8-byte return address is pushed) it is 8 past a multiple of 16:

```formula
rsp_before mod 16 = 0
rsp_entry = rsp_before − 8
rsp_entry mod 16 = 8
rsp_entry = 4096 − 8 = 4088
4088 mod 16 = 8
where
rsp_before: the stack pointer just before the call instruction, in this example 4096 (0x1000)
rsp_entry: the stack pointer on the first instruction of the called function
mod: modulo: the remainder after dividing by 16 (4088 = 255 × 16 + 8)
16: the alignment in bytes that both ABIs require at a call
8: the size of the pushed return address
In words: the call's push leaves rsp 8 bytes off a 16-byte boundary, so a function must move rsp by another 8 (or 24, 40, …) before it makes its own call.
```

That is why the preceding factorial unit’s `fact` is aligned: its single `push rbx` moves `rsp` down another 8 bytes, to 4080 in this example, a multiple of 16 for the inner call. Compilers sometimes `push rax` or `sub rsp, 8` purely to fix alignment. Get it wrong in hand-written code and you may crash in a library function that uses aligned SSE instructions such as `movaps`.

ARM64 is stricter: `sp` itself must be 16-byte aligned whenever it is used as the base of a memory access (the hardware can trap if it is not), so stack allocations normally preserve that alignment. Saving a pair is convenient, but a single register can also be stored in an aligned allocation.

**Red zone.** The System V x86-64 ABI promises that the 128 bytes below `rsp` will not be clobbered by signal handlers. Leaf functions can use that space for locals without adjusting `rsp`. Kernel code is compiled with `-mno-red-zone` because hardware interrupts push data onto the current stack.

## Key takeaways
- A frame pointer offers a stable base when the function maintains one.
- Ordinary System V calls align RSP before CALL, which then pushes eight bytes.
- The System V user-space red zone is not a kernel interrupt-stack guarantee.

## Further reading

- [Call stack — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_stack)

questions.prompt:
A Linux x86-64 function begins like this and later makes a `call`. Which value of `N` keeps the stack correctly aligned for that call?

```
f:
    push  rbp
    mov   rbp, rsp
    sub   rsp, N
```

Assume no other stack adjustments and an ordinary call requiring 16-byte alignment.

options.explanation: On entry `rsp % 16 == 8`. After `push rbp` it is 0. Subtracting 8 would make it 8 again: misaligned at the call.
Not even a multiple of 8, so `rsp` would end up misaligned for 8-byte stores too. The value must be a multiple of 16 here.
Correct. After `push rbp`, `rsp` is a multiple of 16; subtracting any multiple of 16 keeps it that way, which is what the ABI demands just before `call`.
24 = 16 + 8, so this leaves `rsp % 16 == 8` at the call. It would be right for a function with no `push`, not for this one.

questions.workedExample:
In the code, `rsp % 16` is C notation for the remainder when rsp is divided by 16.

1. The rule: `rsp % 16 == 0` immediately before `call`.
2. The caller's `call` pushed an 8-byte return address, so on entry to `f`, `rsp % 16 == 8`.
3. `push rbp` subtracts 8: now `rsp % 16 == 0`.
4. `sub rsp, N` must keep that: N must be a multiple of 16. Of the options, only 16 works.

```formula
rsp_entry mod 16 = 8
(rsp_entry − 8) mod 16 = 0
(rsp_entry − 8 − N) mod 16 = 0
so N mod 16 = 0
(4088 − 8 − 16) mod 16 = 4064 mod 16 = 0
where
rsp_entry: the stack pointer on entry to f, for example 4088
N: the number of bytes `sub rsp, N` reserves
mod: modulo: the remainder after dividing (4064 = 254 × 16, remainder 0)
8: the size of the pushed rbp
16: the alignment the ABI requires at a call
In words: after push rbp the stack is already 16-byte aligned, so whatever f reserves must be a whole number of 16-byte blocks.
```

Compare a function that pushes nothing: it needs `sub rsp, 8` (or 24, 40, ...) to get aligned, which is why you see odd-looking `sub rsp, 8` or a dummy `push rax` in compiler output.

questions.prompt:
On Linux x86-64, a function with nine `long` parameters starts with the classic prologue:

```
h:
    push  rbp
    mov   rbp, rsp
```

Where is the **8th** argument?

options.explanation: That is the 7th argument: just above the return address.
Negative offsets from `rbp` are this function's own locals. Incoming stack arguments are in the caller's frame, at positive offsets.

options.text: `r10`, the next register after `r9`
options.explanation: System V has only six integer argument registers. `r10` is a scratch register (and passes the 4th argument for Linux system calls, not for normal functions).
Correct. `[rbp]` = saved `rbp`, `[rbp+8]` = return address, `[rbp+16]` = 7th, `[rbp+24]` = 8th, `[rbp+32]` = 9th.

questions.workedExample:
1. Arguments 1–6 are in registers; 7, 8 and 9 go on the stack, with the 7th at the lowest address.
2. Before the `call`, the stack looks like (low to high): 7th, 8th, 9th.
3. `call` pushes the return address below the 7th.
4. `push rbp` pushes the saved `rbp` below that, and `mov rbp, rsp` points `rbp` at it.

```
rbp+32  9th arg
rbp+24  8th arg
rbp+16  7th arg
rbp+8   return address
rbp+0   saved rbp
```

```formula
A_k = rbp + 8 × (k − 5)   for k ≥ 7
A_8 = rbp + 8 × 3 = rbp + 24
where
A_k, A_8: the address of argument number k (8 here)
k: the argument's position in the call, counting from 1
rbp: the frame pointer after the prologue, pointing at the saved rbp
5: rbp + 0 and rbp + 8 store the saved rbp and the return address, so argument 7 starts 2 slots up: 7 − 5 = 2
8: each slot is 8 bytes
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: skip the saved rbp and the return address, then count 8 bytes per stack argument from the 7th.
```

questions.prompt: A leaf function in a Linux **user-space** program stores a temporary at `[rsp - 16]` without moving `rsp`. Someone copies the same code into a Linux **kernel** module. What is the right assessment?

options.text: Safe in user space thanks to the 128-byte red zone; unsafe in the kernel, where interrupts push onto the current stack and the kernel is built with `-mno-red-zone`
options.explanation: Correct. System V promises signal handlers won't clobber the 128 bytes below `rsp`. In the kernel, a hardware interrupt can arrive at any moment and write right below `rsp`.

options.text: Fine in both: memory below `rsp` is never touched by anyone else
options.explanation: Below-`rsp` memory is free for anyone who pushes onto the stack. The user-space guarantee is a specific ABI promise, not a law of nature.

options.text: Unsafe in both, because signal handlers always run on the same stack just below `rsp`
options.explanation: The kernel deliberately skips the red zone when it builds a signal frame on the user stack, precisely so this pattern is safe in user space.

options.text: Unsafe in user space, but fine in the kernel because the kernel cannot be interrupted
options.explanation: The kernel can certainly be interrupted. That is exactly why it disables the red zone.

questions.workedExample:
1. The red zone is a System V x86-64 ABI promise: the 128 bytes below `rsp` will not be modified by signal or interrupt handlers.
2. Leaf functions exploit it to skip `sub rsp, N` / `add rsp, N`.
3. In user space, the kernel honours this when delivering signals by placing the signal frame below the red zone.
4. In kernel mode, an interrupt may push its frame onto the current kernel stack directly below `rsp`, destroying the value. Hence `-mno-red-zone`.

Windows x64 has no red zone at all, so the same trick is also wrong there.

lessons.title: Windows, variadic calls and tail-call boundaries
lessons.summary: Recognise platform differences and the conditions behind tail-call and unwind behaviour.
lessons.body:
## Real-world variations

- **Windows x64** uses a different convention: arguments in `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9`; the caller must reserve 32 bytes of "shadow space" on the stack (one 8-byte slot for each of the four register arguments); `rsi` and `rdi` are callee-saved, as are `xmm6`–`xmm15`. Code that crosses the boundary (Wine, JITs, hand-written assembly) must translate.
- **Variadic functions** on System V set `al` to a maximum (0–8) for the number of vector registers used; it need not be the exact count. This lets the callee decide whether to save vector argument registers. On Apple ARM64, anonymous variadic arguments go on the stack (named fixed parameters follow their normal rules), which breaks code that pretends a variadic function is non-variadic.
- **Tail calls.** If a function's last action is a call, the compiler can restore its frame and `jmp` (x86) or `b` (ARM64) to the target instead. The callee returns straight to the original caller, without adding another outstanding return frame; the callee may still use stack space. ABI and language constraints determine whether this transformation is possible.
- **Profiling and unwinding.** Frame pointers simplify walking a compatible chain, while unwind metadata can describe optimized frames without one. A universal performance percentage and blanket claims about distribution package rebuilds are omitted because they require version- and workload-specific evidence.

## Pitfalls

- **Assuming a scratch register survives a call.** After `call`, `rax`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `rsi`, `rdi` and `r8`–`r11` may hold anything.
- **Forgetting to save `x30`** across a nested ARM64 call that must return normally, so `ret` jumps back into the function itself.
- **Misaligning the stack** in hand-written x86-64 code, which can cause a fault in a library using aligned instructions.
- **Using the Linux convention on Windows**, or vice versa, when writing assembly or declaring foreign functions.
- **Mismatched prototypes.** Calling a function through the wrong signature (for example passing an `int` where a `double` is expected) puts the value in the wrong register class entirely.

## Key takeaways
- Windows x64 uses different argument registers and shadow space.
- Variadic arguments need the platform’s special rules.
- An eligible tail call restores the frame and transfers to the next callee.

## Further reading

questions.prompt: A compiler turns `return g(x + 1);` at the end of `f` into a **tail call**. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: `f` tears down its own frame and then jumps (`jmp`/`b`) to `g` instead of calling it
options.explanation: Correct. The call becomes a jump after the epilogue, so `g` reuses `f`'s stack slot.

options.text: `g` returns directly to `f`'s caller
options.explanation: Correct. The return address on the stack (x86) or in `x30` (ARM64) is still the one `f`'s caller set up.

options.text: f necessarily retains a physical stack frame that any debugger can walk while g is running
options.explanation: False: a tail-call optimization removes that frame. Some debuggers can reconstruct a logical tail-call frame using suitable debug information, so absence from every backtrace is not guaranteed.

options.text: Tail calls let tail-recursive functions run in constant stack space
options.explanation: Correct if the recursive calls are actually optimized and per-step stack requirements stay bounded. This avoids stack growth from the recursive call chain, not every possible source of stack exhaustion.

options.text: Tail calls are always possible, even if `f` passed `g` a pointer to one of its own locals
options.explanation: If g needs f’s local object to remain alive, simply discarding its storage would be wrong. The optimizer must preserve the required lifetime; the mere presence of a pointer does not prove it will be used.

questions.workedExample: A valid tail call restores the outgoing function’s saved state and transfers control without adding a new return frame. The callee returns directly to the original caller. Applying this repeatedly to tail recursion avoids growth from that chain. A physical frame disappears, although debug metadata may let a debugger display a logical call. Required object lifetimes and ABI constraints can prevent the transformation.

questions.prompt: You are porting a hand-written assembly routine from Linux x86-64 to **Windows x64**. Which changes are required? Select all that apply.

options.text: Read the first four integer arguments from `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9` instead of `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`
options.explanation: Correct. Windows x64 uses a different, shorter argument register list.

options.text: Before calling another function, reserve 32 bytes of shadow space on the stack
options.explanation: Correct. The Windows caller must leave 32 bytes above the return address for the callee to spill its four register arguments.

options.text: Save and restore `rsi` and `rdi` if the routine uses them
options.explanation: Correct. They are callee-saved on Windows, unlike System V, so trashing them breaks the caller.

options.text: Return integer results in `rcx` instead of `rax`
options.explanation: Both conventions return integers in `rax`. Only the argument registers changed.

options.text: Flip the stack to grow upwards
options.explanation: The stack grows downwards on x86-64 under every mainstream OS. The direction is set by `push`, `call` and `ret`, not by the ABI.

questions.workedExample:
1. Arguments: System V uses `rdi rsi rdx rcx r8 r9`; Windows uses `rcx rdx r8 r9` and then the stack.
2. Shadow space: Windows callers always reserve 32 bytes, even for functions with fewer arguments.
3. Callee-saved set: Windows adds `rsi`, `rdi` and `xmm6`–`xmm15` to the registers you must preserve.
4. Unchanged: return values in `rax`/`xmm0`, 16-byte alignment at calls, downward-growing stack.

Getting even one of these wrong produces crashes that only appear when called from real Windows code, which is why tools like Wine need translation thunks.

lessons.title: Lower an if/else into branches or flags
lessons.summary: Trace branch-based and branch-free implementations of the same conditional.
lessons.body:
The CPU has no idea what a `for` loop, a `switch` or a `struct` is. It has compares, conditional branches, and loads and stores with an address. Everything structured in your source code is *lowered* to those; this translation step is called **compiler lowering**.

Once you know the handful of patterns compilers use, optimised assembly stops looking like noise. You can spot the loop in a profile, see why a `switch` became an indirect jump, and work out from `[rdi + rax*8 + 4]` which field of which array element is being read.

The listings are illustrative scalar implementations using Linux LP64 type sizes and System V x86-64 or AAPCS64 conventions. They are not promises of exact Clang output; version, flags and target change instruction selection. Assume valid object bounds and no signed C arithmetic overflow. Partial dispatch listings explicitly omit case bodies. Try them yourself on [Compiler Explorer](https://godbolt.org/).

## if/else: test, then branch around

One common lowering of an `if` uses a compare that sets flags and a conditional jump that **skips** the body. The jump condition is therefore usually the *inverse* of the source condition. Schematically:

```
// if (x > 0) y = 1; else y = 2;
    test  edi, edi
    jle   .Lelse       # skip if x <= 0
    mov   eax, 1
    jmp   .Ldone
.Lelse:
    mov   eax, 2
.Ldone:
```

When both arms are cheap and have no side effects, the compiler often removes the branch entirely with `cmov` (x86) or `csel` (ARM64). This can trade branch-misprediction costs for evaluating both candidate values; whether it helps depends on the core, dependencies and workload. A universal cycle penalty is omitted because no particular core or measurement is specified.

For this snippet another valid lowering is possible. It notices the result is 1 plus a 0-or-1 flag:

```formula
y = 1 + c
c = 1 if x ≤ 0, otherwise 0
where
y: the result the if/else produces, 1 or 2
x: the input, held in edi
c: the condition turned into a number; `setle` (set if less than or equal) writes it
≤: less than or equal to
In words: a positive x gives 1 + 0 = 1, and anything else gives 1 + 1 = 2, exactly what the if/else computes.
```

```
    xor   eax, eax
    test  edi, edi
    setle al           # al = (x <= 0)
    inc   eax          # 1 or 2
```

No branch, no `cmov`: just flags turned into a number. This illustrates one possible rewrite; inspect actual compiler output to see whether it is used.

## Key takeaways
- Lowering translates source constructs into simpler machine operations.
- A branch can skip a body by testing the opposite condition.
- Conditional moves and SETcc offer alternative lowerings when semantics permit.

## Further reading

- [Data structure alignment — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure_alignment)

- [Loop unrolling — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loop_unrolling)

lessons.title: Guarded loops, pointer walks and optimisation
lessons.summary: Trace scalar sums and recognise loop rotation and strength reduction.
lessons.body:
These illustrative scalar listings use Linux LP64 type sizes: `long` is eight bytes. Arrays must be valid for every accessed element and signed C sums must remain representable. RDI/X0 hold the pointer; RSI/X1 hold the count.

## Loops: the guarded do-while

Here is the canonical array sum:

```
long sum(long *a, long n) {
    long s = 0;
    for (long i = 0; i < n; i++)
        s += a[i];
    return s;
}
```

A naive translation tests `i < n` at the top and jumps back unconditionally at the bottom: two branches per iteration. Compilers can **rotate the loop**: check once on entry whether it runs at all, then put the test at the bottom.

```
sum:
    test  rsi, rsi
    jle   .Lzero          # n <= 0
    xor   ecx, ecx        # i = 0
    xor   eax, eax        # s = 0
.Lloop:
    add   rax, [rdi + 8*rcx]
    inc   rcx             # i++
    cmp   rsi, rcx
    jne   .Lloop          # until i == n
    ret
.Lzero:
    xor   eax, eax
    ret
```

Things to notice:

- The loop body is four instructions with **one** branch, taken every time except the last.
- `a[i]` is a single memory operand: base `rdi`, index `rcx`, scale 8 because a `long` is 8 bytes.
- The exit test became `i != n` rather than `i < n`. Once the guard has established `n > 0`, these are equivalent.

An A64 version turns the index into a moving pointer and a down-counter:

```
sum:
    cmp   x1, #1
    b.lt  .Lzero          // n < 1
    mov   x8, xzr         // s = 0
.Lloop:
    ldr   x9, [x0], #8    // load; +8 bytes
    subs  x1, x1, #1      // n--, set flags
    add   x8, x9, x8
    b.ne  .Lloop          // until n == 0
    // Return the accumulated result.
    mov   x0, x8
    ret
.Lzero:
    mov   x0, #0
    ret
```

The post-indexed load reads and advances the pointer in one instruction, and `subs` both decrements and sets the flags, so no separate compare is needed. Replacing the multiply-based address with a pointer bumped by 8 is classic **strength reduction**: an indexed-address recurrence becomes a pointer increment.

```formula
p_i = a + i × 8
p_{i+1} = p_i + 8
where
p_i: the address of element i
p_{i+1}: the address of the next element
a: the address where the array starts
i: the element index, counting from 0
8: the size of a `long` in bytes
In words: instead of multiplying the index by 8 every time, keep the previous address and add 8; with a = 0x1000, the addresses run 0x1000, 0x1008, 0x1010 and so on.
```

The original scaled addressing did not necessarily require a separate multiply instruction.

> [!tip] Spotting loops in a listing
> Look for a **backward** branch: a conditional jump to a label *above* it. Then inspect the control-flow graph for a cycle; backward branches alone do not prove source-level loop boundaries in arbitrarily laid-out code. In `perf annotate` output, the hot instructions cluster inside it.

### What -O2 and -O3 add

At higher optimisation levels the same loop may grow considerably:

- **Unrolling**: the body is repeated (say four times per iteration) to cut loop overhead, with a cleanup loop for leftovers.
- **Vectorisation**: SIMD instructions (`paddq` on x86, `add v0.2d` on ARM64) add several elements at once. Leftover elements may use a scalar tail, masked vectors or other cleanup.
- **Loop-invariant code motion**: expressions proven invariant may move outside a loop when doing so preserves language semantics and is profitable.

So a five-line C loop can become fifty lines of assembly. A common structure is a guard, main loop and remainder handling; it is not universal.

## Key takeaways
- An entry guard preserves the zero-iteration case.
- A down-counter and post-indexed load can replace explicit indexing.
- Unrolling and vectorisation need remainder handling when applicable.
